meta.blurb: Two people watch two lightning bolts strike a railway track and disagree about whether they struck together. Einstein says both are right. His own short book takes you on to bent starlight and curved space, in plain words.
meta.bible: Albert Einstein: the physicist who wrote this book in 1916 for readers without mathematics; patient, plain and modest. Relativity: the theory in two parts, the Special theory (steady motion) and the General theory (gravity and any motion). Galileo: the Italian who noticed that all steady motion looks alike. Newton: whose law of gravitation the new theory improves. Euclid: the Greek whose geometry is taught in school. Lorentz: Hendrik Lorentz, the Dutch physicist behind the Lorentz transformation. Fizeau: the French physicist who measured light in flowing water. Michelson and Morley: who searched for the Ether and found nothing. Minkowski: Hermann Minkowski, the mathematician of four-dimensional Spacetime. Gauss: Carl Friedrich Gauss, who described curved surfaces with a net of lines. Mercury: the planet nearest the Sun. Berlin and the Potsdamer Platz: Einstein's example of a reference point. Embankment: the raised bank beside a railway track. Key terms: Geometry, Simultaneity, Coordinates, Transformation, Inertia, Gravitation, Equivalence, Acceleration, Perihelion, Eclipse, Spectrum, Spectral, Radium, Pi, Circumference, Diameter. Facts: light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second in empty space; Mercury's orbit has a turning of about 43 seconds of arc a century that Newton's law does not explain; the 1919 eclipse measurements supported the bending of starlight; the universe's true size and shape are left open. Voice and tone: clear, careful, patient and friendly, one idea at a time, with train and lightning examples. Added names: Isaac Newton's laws date from 1687. Bern: the Swiss city where Einstein worked as a patent clerk in 1905. Berlin: where Einstein lived in 1916. Kepler: Johannes Kepler, who found that planets move in ellipses. Maxwell: James Clerk Maxwell, whose theory describes light as a wave of electricity and magnetism. Mach: Ernst Mach, the Austrian physicist and thinker. Bradley: James Bradley, the English astronomer who found the aberration of starlight. Eotvos: Loránd Eötvös, the Hungarian physicist who tested that all things fall alike. Grossmann: Marcel Grossmann, Einstein's friend and a mathematician who helped him. Riemann: Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician of curved spaces. Le Verrier: Urbain Le Verrier, the French astronomer who found Mercury's puzzle in 1859. Vulcan: the planet once imagined inside Mercury's orbit and never found. Eddington: Arthur Eddington, the English astronomer who led the 1919 eclipse test. Dyson: Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal. Principe: the island off West Africa where Eddington watched the 1919 eclipse. Sobral: the town in Brazil where the second 1919 expedition watched. Cleveland: the American city where Michelson and Morley worked. Pythagoras: the Greek whose theorem links the sides of a right triangle. Seeliger: Hugo von Seeliger, the German astronomer who suggested a change to Newton's law. Sun, Earth, Moon, Milky Way. Key terms: Ellipse, Parabola, Sphere, Interferometer, Velocity, Contraction, Dilation, Curvature, Geodesic, Covariance, Euclidean, Riemannian, Newtonian, Galilean, Ether, Equivalence, Redshift, Gravitational, Cosmological, Observatory, Telescope, Photograph, Plates, Corona, Hyades.
chapters: The Cloud and the Falling Stone

beats.scene: Einstein at his desk in Berlin writing a small book for ordinary readers
beats.summary: In 1916 Einstein sits down in Berlin to write a short book that explains his theory to readers without mathematics.

beats.scene: A reader with a cup of tea frowns at a page and keeps going
beats.summary: Einstein asks for patience and a strong will, because the words are plain but the ideas are new.

beats.scene: A road map with three signposts pointing to steady motion, gravity and the universe
beats.summary: The book has three parts: the special theory, the general theory and a look at the universe as a whole.

beats.scene: A clock face and a measuring rod lie side by side on a table
beats.summary: Everyone thinks they know what space and time are, and the book will test this by asking how they are measured.

beats.scene: A scientist weighs a stone on a scale while a pendulum swings
beats.summary: Physics trusts only what can be measured and tested, so every idea must be tied to something we can check.

beats.scene: Isaac Newton beside a falling apple and planets circling in the sky
beats.summary: For more than two hundred years Newton's laws explained so much that few people doubted them.

beats.scene: A young clerk at a patent office desk in Bern with papers around him
beats.summary: In 1905 Einstein, a young clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern, published the special theory of relativity.

beats.scene: Einstein pacing a study at night with notebooks and papers everywhere
beats.summary: The general theory was much harder to build and reached its final form in 1915.

beats.scene: A bird on a moving train seen against a station and a distant cloud
beats.summary: The name relativity points to a simple fact: we always judge motion by comparing it with something else.

beats.scene: A student opens a school geometry book at its first page
beats.summary: Einstein begins with geometry, the oldest and most trusted science of space.

beats.scene: Surveyors stretch a rope between two stakes in a farmer's field
beats.summary: The word geometry comes from Greek words for measuring the earth, and the subject began with practical land measuring.

beats.scene: An ancient Greek teacher writes on a scroll beside a drawn triangle
beats.summary: Euclid, a Greek teacher who lived about 2,300 years ago, arranged geometry as a chain of statements, each resting on the ones before.

beats.scene: A teacher at a blackboard draws two dots joined by one straight line
beats.summary: A few starting statements, called axioms, are accepted without proof, such as that two points have exactly one straight line through them.

beats.scene: A right triangle with a square drawn on each of its three sides
beats.summary: From the axioms a student proves theorems, such as the famous one about the squares on the sides of a right triangle.

beats.scene: A young student smiles at a finished proof on a slate
beats.summary: A proof gives a feeling of complete certainty, which is why people have admired geometry for so long.

beats.scene: A puzzled student stares at a dot and a line drawn on paper
beats.summary: It is hard to say whether the statements of geometry are true, because words like point and line are only loosely tied to real things.

beats.scene: A balance with a logic book on one side, a rod on the other
beats.summary: In pure geometry a statement is true if it follows by logic from the axioms, which says nothing about real objects.

beats.scene: A tight string stretched between two pegs in a garden
beats.summary: To make geometry a science of the real world, Einstein ties its words to things such as a taut string and a stiff rod.

beats.scene: A surveyor with a rod and a tripod measures the corners of a field
beats.summary: Once its words mean real things, geometry becomes a branch of physics and can be tested by measurement.

beats.scene: Builders check a straight wall with a long level as the sun sets
beats.summary: Euclid's geometry works superbly for houses, roads and fields, but that does not prove it holds everywhere.

beats.scene: A cloud hangs above a famous Berlin square on a bright day
beats.summary: Saying that a cloud hangs above the Potsdamer Platz in Berlin gives its position by pointing to a place on the solid earth.

beats.scene: A tall pole stands in the square and reaches up toward the cloud
beats.summary: We can add the height of the cloud by imagining a tall pole that reaches up from the square to the cloud.

beats.scene: Three lines meet at the corner of a room like a frame
beats.summary: Three numbers, such as how far along, how far across and how high, fix any position and are called coordinates.

beats.scene: A ship's navigator marks a position on a sea chart
beats.summary: A navigator at sea also gives a ship's place with numbers, measured from the solid surface of the earth.

beats.scene: A rigid frame of rods rises over a town like scaffolding
beats.summary: Physicists call the solid thing we measure from a body of reference, and every position is given in relation to it.

beats.scene: A cyclist passes marker posts beside a road while a clock ticks
beats.summary: Motion means that the position of an object changes as time goes by, so describing it takes both a place and a time.

beats.scene: A man at a railway carriage window lets a stone fall from his hand
beats.summary: Einstein pictures a man in a moving railway carriage who lets a stone drop without throwing it.

beats.scene: A straight arrow beside a curved arrow, both showing the stone's fall
beats.summary: The man sees the stone fall in a straight line, while a person on the embankment sees it fall along a curve.

beats.scene: Two observers hold different drawings of the same stone's journey
beats.summary: The path of a body has no meaning until we say which body of reference it is measured from.

beats.scene: Einstein studies a pocket watch and a stone side by side
beats.summary: Time has been used so far without being defined, a gap that Einstein promises to come back to.

beats.scene: A smooth ball rolls across a vast sheet of ice with nothing nearby
beats.summary: The law of inertia says that a body far from all others stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed.

beats.scene: A spinning fairground ride throws a ball outward across its floor
beats.summary: The law of inertia does not hold for every body of reference, and those for which it holds are called Galilean.

beats.scene: Passengers lurch forward as a train brakes hard
beats.summary: A train that brakes hard or turns a sharp bend is no longer a Galilean body of reference, because loose objects begin to move.

beats.scene: A train glides along a straight track at an even speed
beats.summary: Steady motion in a straight line, without rotation or jolts, is called uniform translation.

beats.scene: Two trains run side by side on smooth tracks, one passing the other
beats.summary: The restricted principle of relativity says the laws of nature are the same in every Galilean body of reference.

beats.scene: A cabin below deck with a bowl of fish and a dripping bottle
beats.summary: Galileo noticed that in a cabin below deck on a ship moving steadily, no experiment shows whether the ship moves.

beats.scene: The earth circles the sun while a person stands calmly on its surface
beats.summary: The Earth circles the Sun at about thirty kilometres a second, yet we feel nothing because the motion is nearly steady.

beats.scene: A man walks forward along a moving carriage while two arrows show the speeds
beats.summary: The old rule says that a man walking along a moving carriage has the carriage's speed plus his own.

beats.scene: A speedometer shows a hundred beside a small walking figure
beats.summary: With the train at a hundred kilometres an hour and the man walking at five, the old rule gives a hundred and five, or ninety-five if he walks back.

beats.scene: Two clocks, one on a train and one in a station, tick together
beats.summary: The old rule quietly assumes that time and distance are the same for the train and the ground, which nobody had thought to question.

beats.scene: A beam of light crosses a dark sky toward a far-off planet
beats.summary: In empty space light travels at about 300,000 kilometres a second, a speed that is very hard to imagine.

beats.scene: A lightning flash above a town while thunder rumbles a moment later
beats.summary: We see lightning almost at once but hear thunder much later, because sound is far slower than light.

beats.scene: A glowing ring of light circles a globe again and again
beats.summary: In a single second a beam of light could go around the Earth about seven times.

beats.scene: Beams of many colours cross a dark room side by side
beats.summary: Light of every colour has the same speed in empty space, and the speed does not depend on the lamp that made it.

beats.scene: A ray of light runs along an embankment beside a straight railway track
beats.summary: Einstein pictures a ray of light travelling along the embankment at its usual speed.

beats.scene: A train races along the track beside the ray while a passenger looks out
beats.summary: Now a train runs along the track in the same direction as the ray, and a passenger on it wants to measure the ray's speed.

beats.scene: Figures show a train's speed taken away from the speed of light
beats.summary: The old rule for adding speeds says the passenger should find the speed of light minus the speed of the train.

beats.scene: A passenger holds a stopwatch and watches a ray of light run past
beats.summary: The principle of relativity says the law of light must hold for the train just as it holds for the ground, so the passenger should also find the full speed of light.

beats.scene: Two blackboard signs, one for adding speeds, one for light, pointing apart
beats.summary: The old rule for adding speeds and the constant speed of light cannot both be right, and this is the heart of the puzzle.

beats.scene: Einstein at his desk with a pencil, looking hard at the word time
beats.summary: Instead of giving up either idea, Einstein decides to ask what the old rule quietly assumes about time and distance.

beats.scene: A station clock with its small hand at seven as a train rolls in
beats.summary: When we say a train arrives at seven, we mean that the small hand pointing to seven and the arrival happen together.

beats.scene: A rocket bursts over distant hills while a clock ticks in the valley
beats.summary: For an event far away the question is harder, because it is not clear what the same time means in two places.

beats.scene: A man stares through a telescope at a tower clock far across a plain
beats.summary: Looking at a far clock does not help, because light takes time to travel and the delay must be worked out.

beats.scene: Two identical clocks stand far apart, one at each end of a long field
beats.summary: Two clocks that tick at the same rate still need to be set to the same time, and that needs a clear rule.

beats.scene: A flash of light leaves one clock, reaches a mirror and returns
beats.summary: Einstein defines it with light: a signal that goes from A to B and back takes the same time each way.

beats.scene: Lightning strikes two far-apart points on a railway embankment
beats.summary: Einstein pictures two lightning strokes, one at place A and one at place B, far apart on the embankment.

beats.scene: An observer stands at the midpoint between two flashes and sees both at once
beats.summary: A man standing exactly midway between A and B sees both flashes at the same moment, so he says they were simultaneous.

beats.scene: A passenger on a moving train rushes toward the flash from B
beats.summary: A passenger riding the train, midway between A and B, moves toward the light from B and away from the light from A.

beats.scene: The passenger frowns at a notebook, sure that B was struck first
beats.summary: The passenger meets the light from B first, so he says that stroke B came before stroke A.

beats.scene: Two observers on the track and the train point in different directions
beats.summary: Each observer is right in his own body of reference, so there is no single now that is true for everybody.

beats.scene: A stiff rod lies on a workbench beside a ruler
beats.summary: A length is easy to find when the rod is at rest, because we simply lay a ruler along it.

beats.scene: A passenger lays a ruler along the floor of a moving carriage
beats.summary: A passenger riding with a rod on the train can measure it in the usual way and gets one answer.

beats.scene: A man on the embankment marks the two ends of a passing train
beats.summary: A man on the ground marks the places where the two ends of the train are at the same moment, then measures the gap between the marks.

beats.scene: Two measuring tapes with different numbers stretch beside the same carriage
beats.summary: The two methods give different lengths, because the man on the ground and the passenger disagree about which moments are simultaneous.

beats.scene: Hendrik Lorentz at a blackboard covered with neat rows of symbols
beats.summary: The Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz found a rule, now named after him, that turns one observer's place and time into another's.

beats.scene: A carriage seen from outside looks squeezed along its direction of travel
beats.summary: Seen from outside, a moving rod is shorter along its line of motion, and the faster it goes the shorter it gets.

beats.scene: A rod moving at nearly the speed of light shrinks to half its length
beats.summary: At about 260,000 kilometres a second, a moving rod would measure only half its length at rest.

beats.scene: Two clocks side by side, one ticking slowly as it speeds past
beats.summary: A moving clock also runs slowly as seen from outside, and at that same speed it would tick at half the usual rate.

beats.scene: A passenger smiles at his own ruler and clock, which look quite normal
beats.summary: To the passenger riding along, his own rods and clocks look quite normal, and the strange effects appear only when two observers compare.

beats.scene: A fast express train beside a tiny atom drawn far larger than life
beats.summary: At the speed of a train the effects are tens of thousands of times smaller than an atom, so nobody notices them.

beats.scene: A speed dial with its needle stopped at the speed of light
beats.summary: According to the theory, nothing can travel faster than light, so light's speed is a limit for every body.

beats.scene: A fast train with a shrunken carriage and a slow clock inside
beats.summary: As a body nears the speed of light the effects grow extreme, and a rod would shrink toward nothing as its clock slowed to a crawl.

beats.scene: Two trains of arrows on a chalkboard, one at half the speed of light
beats.summary: Speeds do not simply add: a train going half the speed of light with a man walking forward at half that speed gives about eight-tenths of light's speed.

beats.scene: A chalkboard sum ending just short of the speed of light
beats.summary: Whatever two speeds below the speed of light are combined, the answer stays below it.

beats.scene: A train beam shines ahead from a fast carriage toward a distant station
beats.summary: A lamp on a very fast train sends a beam forward, and both the passenger and the man at the station find light moving at its usual speed.

beats.scene: Hippolyte Fizeau beside two pipes of rushing water and mirrors
beats.summary: In 1851 the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau sent beams of light through tubes of flowing water.

beats.scene: A beam of light slows as it enters a glass tube of still water
beats.summary: In still water light goes at about 225,000 kilometres a second, and the old rule said that flowing water should add its own speed in full.

beats.scene: Fizeau reading a scale on his instrument with a puzzled smile
beats.summary: Fizeau found that the water carries the light along only partly, and the new rule for adding speeds gives exactly this result.

beats.scene: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley with a stone table and bright lamps
beats.summary: In 1887 Michelson and Morley in Cleveland searched for the ether, the invisible stuff thought to carry light, and found no sign that the Earth moves through it.

beats.scene: An empty hall of space with a beam of light crossing it unaided
beats.summary: Einstein shows that light needs no ether to carry it, and the empty space around us is enough.

beats.scene: Three old experiments laid out on a table like pieces of evidence
beats.summary: The special theory grew out of the theory of electricity and light by Maxwell and Lorentz, and old experiments fit it well.

beats.scene: A telescope tilted slightly to follow a star as the Earth moves
beats.summary: In 1727 the English astronomer James Bradley found that stars seem to shift a little in the course of a year, and the theory explains this.

beats.scene: A sieve catching wrong laws while correct ones pass through
beats.summary: The theory is also a guide: every general law of nature must keep its form under the Lorentz transformation.

beats.scene: A metal bar glowing with heat beside a pair of delicate scales
beats.summary: A body that takes in energy becomes a little heavier, so mass and energy are really one thing.

beats.scene: A blackboard bearing a short, famous line with an M and a C squared
beats.summary: The energy held in a mass equals the mass multiplied by the speed of light twice over, a very large number.

beats.scene: A single gram weight beside a great city glowing at night
beats.summary: One gram of matter holds about as much energy as twenty-five million kilowatt-hours, more than a family would use in thousands of years.

beats.scene: A small glass tube of radium glowing faintly in the dark
beats.summary: Radium gives off energy as it slowly changes, and in principle it loses a little mass as it does so.

beats.scene: Two big books, one labelled mass and one labelled energy, joined into one
beats.summary: The old law that mass is never lost and the old law that energy is never lost now become a single law.

beats.scene: Hermann Minkowski lecturing to a hall of students in 1908
beats.summary: In 1908 the German mathematician Hermann Minkowski, who had once taught Einstein, showed that space and time join in a single world of four dimensions.

beats.scene: A single event marked by a pin on a map beside a clock
beats.summary: Every event has four numbers, three for where it happens and one for when, and the world is a four-dimensional whole.

beats.scene: A train gliding in a straight line past a quiet field
beats.summary: The special theory covers only steady motion in a straight line, and Einstein now asks whether that is enough.

beats.scene: A car swerving round a bend while a rocket lifts off beside it
beats.summary: Real motion is rarely steady: cars speed up and brake, and planets travel in curves.

beats.scene: A row of Galilean bodies of reference stands apart from a spinning one
beats.summary: In the old physics the Galilean bodies of reference are favoured, because only for them do the laws take their simple form.

beats.scene: Einstein frowning at a drawing of favoured and unfavoured bodies
beats.summary: Einstein feels uneasy, because nature seems to give no reason for preferring steady motion to any other kind.

beats.scene: Two fluid bodies float in empty space, one round and one flattened
beats.summary: Einstein borrows an example from Ernst Mach with two fluid bodies in empty space turning around the line between them, one round and one flattened.

beats.scene: A large invisible frame of absolute space around the two bodies
beats.summary: Newton's answer is that one body turns in absolute space, an invisible and unchanging thing that nobody can see.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over a starry sky, searching for the real cause
beats.summary: Einstein argues that the cause of the flattening should be something that can be observed, not an unseen space.

beats.scene: A wide door opening onto every possible kind of motion
beats.summary: The general principle of relativity says that all bodies of reference are equally good for stating the laws of nature.

beats.scene: A falling stone, a swinging pendulum and a planet in orbit side by side
beats.summary: To build such a theory Einstein must first understand gravity, which acts on all things in the same way.

beats.scene: The moon circling the Earth beside the Earth circling the sun
beats.summary: Newton's law says that every body attracts every other, with a force that grows weaker as the distance grows.

beats.scene: A stone leaves a hand and drops toward the ground
beats.summary: A stone that is let go falls to the ground, because the Earth has a gravitational field that pulls on it.

beats.scene: A feather and a coin drop together in a tall glass tube
beats.summary: In air a feather drifts down slowly, but once the air is pumped out, a feather and a coin fall together.

beats.scene: Galileo above a leaning tower watching two balls fall
beats.summary: A famous story says that Galileo dropped a heavy and a light ball from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, but the tale may be only a legend.

beats.scene: A heavy cart is hard to push while a light cart rolls easily
beats.summary: A heavy body is hard to start or stop, and the size of this resistance is its inertial mass.

beats.scene: A spring scale holds a heavy sack and a light sack
beats.summary: A heavy body is also pulled harder by gravity, and the size of this pull is tied to its gravitational mass.

beats.scene: Two weights fall side by side, one big and one small
beats.summary: Because the two masses are equal, a heavy body is pulled more strongly but also resists more, so the two effects cancel and all bodies fall alike.

beats.scene: A puzzled scientist with a question mark above two jars
beats.summary: The old physics treated the equality of the two masses as a plain fact with no explanation, and Einstein finds this unsatisfying.

beats.scene: A delicate twisting balance in a hall in Budapest
beats.summary: The Hungarian physicist Loránd Eötvös tested the equality with a twisting balance and found no difference, to better than one part in a million.

beats.scene: A signpost reading why, pointing toward hidden depths
beats.summary: Einstein thinks that nature is giving a hint, and that a good theory should explain the equality and not just accept it.

beats.scene: Gravity and a pushing hand drawn as two arrows meeting at one point
beats.summary: The equal fall of all bodies suggests that gravity and a steady push may somehow be the same thing.

beats.scene: A large wooden chest drifting in empty space among far-off stars
beats.summary: Einstein pictures a large chest, like a small room, floating in empty space far from the stars and every other heavy body.

beats.scene: A rope tied to a hook on the lid of the chest
beats.summary: A being outside the chest fastens a rope to a hook on the lid and pulls it with a steady force, so that the chest rises with ever-growing speed.

beats.scene: A man inside the chest stands with his feet pressed to the floor
beats.summary: The man inside feels the floor pressing against his feet, just as he would on the ground on Earth.

beats.scene: A stone drops from the man's hand toward the floor of the chest
beats.summary: When the man lets go of a stone, the floor rushes up to meet it, and to him the stone simply falls, whatever its weight.

beats.scene: An outside observer sees the stone drift straight while the floor rises
beats.summary: An observer outside says that the stone does not fall at all, but the chest accelerates upward past it.

beats.scene: Two arrows labelled gravity and acceleration pointing at the same chest
beats.summary: Neither man can prove the other wrong, and from inside a closed chest no experiment can tell gravity from acceleration.

beats.scene: A weight hangs from a rope fixed to the ceiling of the chest
beats.summary: A weight hanging from the ceiling pulls the rope tight, and the man says that gravity does it, while the outside observer says that the weight resists being pulled along.

beats.scene: Two scales marked inertial mass and gravitational mass balance exactly
beats.summary: In this picture the equality of the two masses is no longer a mystery, because the same property of a body shows itself as weight and as resistance.

beats.scene: A beam of light crosses the chest from one wall to the other
beats.summary: A ray of light that crosses the chest sideways travels straight for the outside observer, but the chest rises while it crosses, so it seems to curve downward inside.

beats.scene: A tiny curved line on a wall beside a huge glowing sun
beats.summary: Across a small room the bending is far too small to see, so only a very large mass such as the Sun could show it.

beats.scene: Two clocks, one at the foot of a tall tower, one at the top
beats.summary: The theory says that clocks run more slowly where gravity is stronger, though on Earth the difference is far too small to notice.

beats.scene: A large flat disc turning steadily in empty space with a tiny observer
beats.summary: To test Euclid's geometry, Einstein pictures a large flat disc that turns steadily around its centre in empty space.

beats.scene: A person on the turning disc is pressed toward its rim
beats.summary: A person standing on the turning disc feels a force pushing him outward, and by equivalence this is like a gravitational field.

beats.scene: A small rod laid end to end around the edge of the disc
beats.summary: The person on the disc wants to measure the circle's edge and its width with small rods, just as a school student would.

beats.scene: A rod laid along the radius, at right angles to the turning
beats.summary: A rod laid along the radius moves at right angles to its length, so the outside observer sees no shortening and the width is measured as usual.

beats.scene: Many shortened rods along the rim fit around the disc
beats.summary: A rod laid along the rim moves along its length, so it seems shortened from outside, and more of them are needed to go around.

beats.scene: A circle with the ratio of rim to width written as more than pi
beats.summary: On the turning disc the rim measures more than the usual number times the width, so Euclid's geometry does not hold there.

beats.scene: A clock at the centre of the disc and another at its rim
beats.summary: A clock at the rim moves quickly as seen from outside, so it runs more slowly than a clock at the centre.

beats.scene: Two clocks on the disc show different times as they tick
beats.summary: The disc observer agrees that a clock far from the centre runs slowly, so in this gravitational field time depends on place.

beats.scene: A broken grid of rods and clocks bending out of shape
beats.summary: In a gravitational field the old way of marking out place and time with ordinary rods and clocks fails, and a new method is needed.

beats.scene: A flat marble table with a drawn triangle and a ruler
beats.summary: On a flat table top Euclid's geometry works perfectly, with straight lines, right angles and triangles in the usual way.

beats.scene: A smooth round hill with a grid of straight lines slipping off it
beats.summary: On a curved surface such as a hill or a ball we cannot lay straight rods in a perfect square grid.

beats.scene: A globe with a triangle running from the pole to the equator and back
beats.summary: On a globe a triangle can have three right angles: go from the North Pole down to the equator, a quarter of the way along it, and back up.

beats.scene: A circle drawn around the pole of a globe, with a string for width
beats.summary: A circle drawn on a ball, measured along the surface, has a rim shorter than the usual number times its width.

beats.scene: Flat creatures on a ball peering at the line of its horizon
beats.summary: Imagine flat creatures who live on a ball and cannot look up or down, who could still find that their world is curved by measuring.

beats.scene: Carl Friedrich Gauss writing at a desk in a German study
beats.summary: The German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss found a way to describe a curved surface without ever leaving it.

beats.scene: A curved surface covered with a net of wavy lines, each carrying a number
beats.summary: Gauss laid a net of curves of any shape on the surface and gave each curve a number, so that every point has two numbers.

beats.scene: Two nearby points joined by a tiny line with a formula beside it
beats.summary: The distance between two nearby points can be worked out from their two numbers by a rule that belongs to the surface.

beats.scene: A rubber sheet stretched and bent with its net of lines still drawn
beats.summary: The net may be bent and stretched in any way, and the whole geometry of the surface can still be found by using the numbers alone.

beats.scene: Bernhard Riemann with a many-sided diagram on a blackboard
beats.summary: Gauss's pupil Bernhard Riemann went further in 1854 and made a geometry for curved spaces of any number of dimensions.

beats.scene: A cube of space with a clock fixed at each corner
beats.summary: In the special theory space and time make one four-dimensional world, and rods and clocks of an ordinary kind give the four numbers of any event.

beats.scene: A bent grid of rods and clocks that no longer match up
beats.summary: In a gravitational field rods and clocks no longer behave in the old way, so the old method of giving numbers to events breaks down.

beats.scene: A drawing of events as dots with four number tags attached
beats.summary: Gauss's idea can be stretched to four dimensions, giving every event four numbers in a net laid over space and time together.

beats.scene: Four dials, one for each number, with none of them marked as a clock
beats.summary: The four numbers are only labels, like house numbers, and the time number need not be read from any clock.

beats.scene: A net of curves wrapped around a swirling cloud of dots
beats.summary: Any fair way of labelling events with four numbers is allowed, however much the net is twisted or stretched.

beats.scene: A page of text with the new principle printed on it
beats.summary: Einstein's general principle says that all Gaussian coordinate systems are essentially equivalent for stating the general laws of nature.

beats.scene: A law written in a form that fits any net, like a stretchy glove
beats.summary: A law of nature must therefore be written so that it keeps its form in every system, which is called general covariance.

beats.scene: Two particles meet at a point, a clock hand touches a mark
beats.summary: All that physics really records are meetings, such as two particles at one point or a clock hand beside a mark.

beats.scene: Two maps of the same crossroads, drawn with different grids
beats.summary: A meeting stays a meeting whatever labels the net gives it, just as a crossroads stays a crossroads on any map.

beats.scene: A smooth glove of numbers pulled over the whole moving world
beats.summary: The numbers no longer mean lengths and times by themselves, but a rule tells how to turn them into distances, and the theory is ready for gravity.

beats.scene: A smooth world map with a hollow dip near a heavy ball
beats.summary: In the general theory the geometry of the four-dimensional world is not the same everywhere, and it changes from place to place.

beats.scene: A heavy sphere pressing a hollow into a stretched sheet
beats.summary: The presence of matter curves the world around it, and this curving is what we call gravity.

beats.scene: A marble curving across a stretched rubber sheet near a heavy ball
beats.summary: A body left to itself follows the straightest possible path in the curved world, much like a marble rolling past a dent, though the real curving involves time as well as space.

beats.scene: The Earth circling the Sun along a smooth curved track
beats.summary: A planet is not pulled by a rope from the Sun but follows the straightest path through the world that the Sun's mass has curved.

beats.scene: Einstein at a blackboard writing a set of long equations in 1915
beats.summary: In 1915 Einstein found the equations that link the curving of the world to the matter and energy in it.

beats.scene: Newton's apple falling beside Einstein's curved grid
beats.summary: Where gravity is weak and speeds are slow, the new equations give almost exactly Newton's law of gravitation.

beats.scene: Two near-identical curves, one slightly different from the other
beats.summary: The two laws are not identical, and the small differences can be tested by observing the sky.

beats.scene: A beam of light bending as it passes a heavy mass
beats.summary: Energy has mass, so light itself has a tiny weight, and gravity bends its path.

beats.scene: A glove of numbers fits the world however it is twisted
beats.summary: The equations keep their form in every system of Gaussian coordinates, so the general principle of relativity is satisfied.

beats.scene: A flat school desk beside the curved sky above the Earth
beats.summary: Near the Earth the world is almost flat, which is why Euclid's geometry works so well in school and in building.

beats.scene: A dark sky crowded with stars above a quiet hill
beats.summary: Einstein now looks at the universe as a whole and asks how the stars are scattered through space.

beats.scene: A climber on a mountain gazes at the pale band of the Milky Way
beats.summary: The old picture, built on Newton's ideas, took space to be endless and Euclidean, with no limit in any direction.

beats.scene: A bright island of stars floating in a vast dark ocean
beats.summary: Suppose the stars form a single island in endless empty space, and ask what would happen to it over a very long time.

beats.scene: Stars and rays of light drifting away from the island into the dark
beats.summary: In that picture light and stars would slowly escape into the void, and the island would dwindle, which Einstein finds hard to accept.

beats.scene: Stars spread evenly through all of space, one beside every other
beats.summary: Suppose instead that stars are spread evenly through endless space, so that the universe never thins out.

beats.scene: A pair of scales tipped wildly by pulls from every direction
beats.summary: Then Newton's law gives a muddle, because the pull on a body from endless matter has no clear value.

beats.scene: Hugo von Seeliger at a telescope with a long page of calculations
beats.summary: The astronomer Hugo von Seeliger suggested changing Newton's law so that gravity fades faster at great distances.

beats.scene: A signpost with a hand-drawn arrow marked invented
beats.summary: Einstein points out that this change was made up only to avoid the trouble, and no fact in the sky supports it.

beats.scene: A ruler stretching beyond the page into endless space
beats.summary: Both pictures lean on the idea that space is endless and Euclidean, but Euclid's geometry is now only one possibility.

beats.scene: A question mark glowing in the darkness beyond the last star
beats.summary: Perhaps the universe can be limited in size without having any edge, and this thought opens a new road.

beats.scene: A small globe held in a hand against a dark background
beats.summary: The surface of a ball has a limited area, yet it has no edge, which is what finite but unbounded means.

beats.scene: Tiny flat creatures walking round and round a vast ball
beats.summary: Flat creatures living on a ball could walk for ever without meeting a wall, even though their world has a limited size.

beats.scene: A string stretched from a pole to make circles on the globe
beats.summary: The creatures could draw circles and measure them, and for big circles they would find the rims shorter than Euclid says.

beats.scene: A triangle on the globe with three right-angled corners
beats.summary: They could also measure triangles and find that the three angles add up to more than two right angles.

beats.scene: A tiny patch of ground that looks flat beside a huge curved horizon
beats.summary: On a very large ball a small region looks flat, just as people once thought that the Earth itself was flat.

beats.scene: A glowing three-dimensional grid of space curved into a gentle ball
beats.summary: Our space might be curved in the same way, closed in on itself, although we cannot picture it.

beats.scene: A traveller walking straight ahead and arriving back at his own front door
beats.summary: In a closed space a traveller going straight on for ever would come back to the place he started from.

beats.scene: A ray of light leaving a lamp and curving round to return
beats.summary: In principle even a ray of light would come back, though the journey would take unimaginably long.

beats.scene: A heavier cloud of stars pulling the glowing space into a smaller ball
beats.summary: The size of a closed universe would depend on how much matter it holds, and in 1916 that was not known well enough.

beats.scene: A telescope pointing toward the deepest, darkest part of the sky
beats.summary: Whether our space is closed is a question for observation, and thought alone cannot settle it.

beats.scene: A sun inside an oval ring with a small planet on it
beats.summary: Johannes Kepler found that each planet travels in an oval path called an ellipse, with the Sun at a special point inside it.

beats.scene: An apple and a planet linked by a single chalk line on a board
beats.summary: Newton's law explains Kepler's findings, and for one planet alone it gives an ellipse that never turns.

beats.scene: The small planet Mercury racing close to a huge blazing Sun
beats.summary: Mercury is the planet nearest to the Sun, and its closest point to the Sun, called the perihelion, is the key to the puzzle.

beats.scene: Venus, Earth and Jupiter pulling gently on tiny Mercury
beats.summary: The pulls of the other planets make Mercury's ellipse turn slowly round the Sun, and Newton's law can work out how much.

beats.scene: Urbain Le Verrier bent over a table of figures in a Paris observatory
beats.summary: In 1859 the French astronomer Urbain Le Verrier found that the real turning is a little larger than Newton's law allows.

beats.scene: A tiny angle drawn on a page beside a great circle of the sky
beats.summary: The leftover is about 43 seconds of arc in a century, so small that a full extra turn would need about three million years.

beats.scene: A telescope pointed at the Sun in a sky darkened by an eclipse
beats.summary: Astronomers imagined a planet called Vulcan, closer to the Sun than Mercury, and searched for it for years without finding it.

beats.scene: Einstein at a desk checking a result with delight
beats.summary: In 1915 Einstein used his new equations on a planet near the Sun and found that they give just the extra turning that Mercury shows.

beats.scene: Mercury and Venus side by side with turning arrows of different sizes
beats.summary: The effect is smaller for the farther planets, so Mercury is the best test of all.

beats.scene: A scale balancing a single result against a long rule
beats.summary: The theory explained the old puzzle without any change or adjustment, and this made the success especially convincing.

beats.scene: A ray of starlight bending as it grazes the edge of the Sun
beats.summary: Einstein's theory says that a ray of starlight passing close to the Sun is bent by a little under two seconds of arc.

beats.scene: The black disc of the Moon covering the Sun, with stars shining around it
beats.summary: Stars near the Sun can be seen only in a total eclipse, when the Moon hides the Sun and the sky grows dark.

beats.scene: Two ships setting out from England toward Africa and Brazil
beats.summary: The astronomers Frank Dyson and Arthur Eddington planned two expeditions to watch the eclipse of 29 May 1919, one to Principe and one to Sobral.

beats.scene: Eddington on Principe watching clouds thin above a row of cameras
beats.summary: On Principe it rained that morning, but the clouds thinned just before the eclipse, and Eddington's team took their photographs.

beats.scene: Glass plates showing a field of stars in the constellation Taurus
beats.summary: The plates showed the bright stars of the Hyades, which were compared with plates of the same stars taken at night.

beats.scene: A packed lecture hall in London listening to a speaker
beats.summary: In November 1919 the results were announced in London: the stars seemed pushed outward by about the amount Einstein predicted, although the measurements were not very exact.

beats.scene: A glowing yellow light from the Sun with its colours shifting slightly toward red
beats.summary: Light leaving a strong gravitational field is shifted slightly toward the red end of the spectrum, and later experiments confirmed it.

beats.scene: An empty stage with a large still platform being taken away
beats.summary: The theory removes Newton's idea of a still, absolute space and of a time that flows in the same way for everybody.

beats.scene: A small book and the two theories drawn as two steps of a staircase
beats.summary: Despite its name, relativity says that the speed of light and the laws of nature are the same for everybody, and the special theory deals with steady motion while the general theory adds gravity.

beats.scene: A reader closing the book with a smile in the evening light
beats.summary: Einstein ends by hoping that the book gives its reader a happy hour of thought, and that his theory stays open to new tests.

A1A2: In 1916 Einstein wrote a small book about his new ideas.
Einstein asks the reader for patience and a strong will.
The book has three parts: steady motion, gravity and the universe.
We all think we know what space and time are.
Physics is a science that trusts only what we can measure.
For over two hundred years, Newton's laws worked very well.
In 1905 Einstein was a young clerk in an office in Bern.
The general theory took Einstein many more years of hard work.
We always say how fast something moves compared with something else.
Einstein begins with geometry, the oldest and most trusted science of space.
The word geometry comes from Greek words meaning earth measurement.
Euclid, a Greek teacher, put geometry in a clear order long ago.
Two points always have exactly one straight line between them.
Students use these rules to prove facts about triangles and squares.
A good proof gives us a strong feeling of certainty.
It is hard to say if these rules are really true.
In pure geometry, a rule is true if it follows from earlier rules.
To measure the real world, we use real things, such as a tight string.
Then geometry becomes a science, and we can test it by measuring.
For houses, roads and fields, the rules of Euclid work very well.
A cloud hangs above the Potsdamer Platz, a square in Berlin.
A tall pole standing in the square can measure how high the cloud is.
Three numbers are enough to say exactly where something is.
A ship's captain also uses numbers to say where the ship is.
We call the solid thing we measure from a body of reference.
A thing is moving when its place changes as time passes.
A man on a train drops a stone from the window.
The man sees a straight fall, but people on the ground see a curve.
So a path means nothing until we say what we measure it against.
So far, Einstein has used the word time without explaining it carefully.
A ball far from everything keeps rolling straight at a steady speed.
This law is not true for every place we choose to measure from.
When a train brakes hard, loose things on it start to move.
Straight motion at an even speed, without turns or bumps, is called steady.
The laws of nature look the same on every steadily moving train.
Galileo said that inside a ship's cabin, nobody can feel steady motion.
The Earth races around the Sun, but we feel nothing at all.
Old physics says a walking man's speed adds to the train's speed.
A train goes a hundred kilometres an hour and the man walks five more.
This rule quietly assumes that time is the same for everyone.
Light moves very fast, about 300,000 kilometres every second.
We see lightning at once, but thunder reaches us later.
In one second, light could go around the Earth seven times.
Light of every colour has the same speed in empty space.
Imagine a ray of light running along the bank beside a railway.
A train runs beside the ray, and a passenger wants to measure it.
Old physics says the passenger sees light slower, by the train's speed.
But the laws of nature must be the same on the train.
These two ideas cannot both be true, and that is the puzzle.
Einstein decides to look hard at what we mean by time.
When we say the train comes at seven, we mean two things happen together.
It is not so clear what the same time means far away.
We cannot just look at a far clock, because light takes time to arrive.
Two clocks with the same speed still need to be set together.
Einstein uses light: a flash goes there and back in equal times.
Imagine two bolts of lightning that hit the bank far apart.
A man standing exactly halfway sees both flashes at the same moment.
A passenger on the train moves toward one flash and away from the other.
The passenger meets the light from B first, so he says B came first.
Both men are right, so there is no single now for everybody.
We find a rod's length by laying a ruler along it.
A passenger on the train does this and finds one answer.
A man on the ground marks both ends of the train together.
The two ways of measuring do not give the same answer.
Lorentz, a Dutch scientist, found a rule that turns one view into another.
Seen from outside, a moving rod is shorter than it is at rest.
A rod moving very, very fast would be only half as long.
A moving clock also runs slowly when seen from outside.
The passenger sees nothing odd about his own ruler or clock.
At the speed of a train, the changes are far too small to see.
Nothing can ever go faster than the speed of light.
As a body nears that speed, strange things happen to its length and time.
Speeds do not simply add up, so half plus half is not one.
Two speeds below the speed of light always give another one below it.
A lamp on a very fast train still gives light at its usual speed.
In 1851 a French scientist named Fizeau sent light through moving water.
Light moves more slowly in water, at about 225,000 kilometres a second.
Fizeau found that moving water carries light along only a little.
In 1887 two men searched for the ether and found nothing.
Einstein shows that light needs no ether, only empty space.
Einstein's theory grew from the study of electricity and light.
In 1727 Bradley saw stars move a little in the sky.
The new theory explains this movement of the stars in a simple way.
A body that takes in energy becomes a little heavier.
The energy in a mass is the mass times the speed of light twice.
One gram of matter holds a huge amount of energy.
Radium gives out energy and loses a tiny part of its weight.
Two old laws about mass and energy now become one law.
In 1908 Minkowski showed that space and time belong together.
Every event has four numbers: three for place and one for time.
The first theory covers only steady motion in a straight line.
But real motion is often not steady: cars brake and planets curve.
In old physics, steadily moving trains were treated as special.
Einstein is not happy, because nature gives no reason for this.
Imagine two bodies in empty space, one round and one flat.
Newton said the flat one turns in a space that never moves.
Einstein says the cause must be something we can actually see.
All kinds of motion should be equally good for stating the laws.
To do this, Einstein must first understand gravity.
Newton said that everything in the world pulls on everything else.
When we let go of a stone, it falls to the ground.
In a tube with no air, a feather and a coin fall together.
A story says Galileo dropped two balls from a very tall tower.
A heavy cart is hard to push, and that is its resistance.
A heavy body is also pulled harder by the Earth.
The two effects cancel, so heavy and light bodies fall alike.
Old physics could not explain why the two are equal.
A Hungarian scientist tested this with a very careful balance.
Einstein thinks this is a hint, and a good theory must explain it.
Maybe gravity and a steady push are really the same thing.
Einstein imagines a big chest floating in empty space.
Someone outside pulls a rope fixed to the chest with a steady force.
The man inside feels the floor pressing on his feet.
He lets go of a stone, and it falls to the floor.
A man outside says the floor rose up to meet the stone.
Nobody inside can tell gravity from a steady push.
A weight hangs from the ceiling, and the rope pulls tight.
So heavy things pull and resist in exactly the same way.
A ray of light crossing the chest seems to curve down.
In a small room the bend is far too small to see.
Clocks run more slowly where gravity is stronger.
Einstein imagines a big flat disc turning round in empty space.
A person on the disc feels a push outward, like gravity.
He measures the edge and the width of the disc with small rods.
A rod laid along the width stays the same length.
Rods laid along the edge look shorter from outside.
So the edge is longer than Euclid's geometry says it should be.
A clock at the edge runs more slowly than one at the centre.
So in this field of force, time depends on the place.
The old way of measuring place and time does not work here.
On a flat table, Euclid's geometry works perfectly.
On a curved surface, we cannot lay out a perfect grid.
On a globe, a triangle can have three right angles.
A circle on a ball has a shorter rim than we expect.
Flat creatures on a ball could find out their world is curved.
A German mathematician named Gauss found a new way to describe curved surfaces.
Gauss drew a net of curves on the surface and gave each a number.
From the two numbers, we can work out the distance between points.
The net can bend and stretch, and the numbers still work.
Riemann went further and made geometry for curved spaces of any size.
In the first theory, rods and clocks give four numbers for every event.
In a field of gravity, rods and clocks do not work in the old way.
Gauss's idea can give every event four numbers.
The four numbers are only labels, like house numbers.
Any fair way of giving the numbers is allowed.
Einstein says that all such systems are equally good.
So a law of nature must keep its form in every system.
All we really observe are meetings, like a clock hand meeting a mark.
A meeting stays a meeting, whatever numbers we give it.
The numbers now need a rule to turn them into distances.
In the new theory, the shape of the world changes from place to place.
Matter curves the world around it, and this curve is gravity.
A body left alone follows the straightest path through this curved world.
The Earth is not pulled by a rope but follows a curved path.
In 1915 Einstein found the equations that connect matter and curves.
For weak gravity and slow motion, the equations give almost Newton's law.
The two laws are not quite the same, and we can test them.
Light has a little weight, so gravity bends its path.
The equations work in every system of numbers.
Near the Earth, space is almost flat, so school geometry works well.
Einstein now asks how the stars are spread through space.
The old picture said that space is endless and has no edge.
Suppose all the stars form one island in endless empty space.
Light and stars would slowly drift away, and the island would shrink.
Or suppose that stars are spread evenly through endless space.
Then the pull on any one body cannot be worked out.
Seeliger suggested changing Newton's law so gravity fades faster.
But this change was made only to avoid the trouble.
Both pictures rely on space that is endless and flat.
Perhaps space can be limited without having an edge.
The surface of a ball has no edge, but it is not endless.
Flat creatures on a ball can walk for ever without meeting a wall.
On a big circle, they would find the rim is too short.
They would also find that the angles of a triangle add up to too much.
On a very large ball, a small part looks flat.
Our space may be curved in the same way.
A traveller who goes straight on would come back to his home.
Even a ray of light might return after a very long journey.
How big such a world is depends on how much matter it holds.
We must use telescopes to answer this question, not just thought.
Kepler found that each planet moves along an oval path.
Newton's law gives an oval that never turns for a single planet.
Mercury is the planet nearest to the Sun.
The pull of the other planets makes its oval turn slowly.
In 1859 a Frenchman found that it turns a little too much.
The extra turn is tiny, about forty-three seconds of angle in a century.
People imagined a planet called Vulcan, but nobody ever found it.
In 1915 Einstein found the extra turn using his new equations.
For the farther planets, the effect is smaller still.
The theory explained the puzzle without any change to fit it.
Einstein's theory says that a ray from a star bends near the Sun.
We can see stars near the Sun only in a total eclipse.
In 1919 two teams went to watch the eclipse far from home.
On the island of Principe, it rained, but the clouds cleared in time.
They photographed the stars and compared them with night photographs.
The stars had moved by about the amount Einstein had said.
Light leaving the Sun is shifted a little toward red.
The theory takes away Newton's still space and one time for all.
Relativity says that the speed of light and nature's laws are the same for all.
Einstein hopes that his book gave you a happy hour of thought.
B1B2: In 1916 the physicist Albert Einstein sat down in Berlin to write a small book. He wanted ordinary readers, even those who knew no mathematics, to understand his new ideas about space and time.
Einstein warns that his book needs patience and a strong will. The words are plain, but the ideas are new, so they cannot be rushed.
Einstein builds his small book in three clear parts, one on top of the other. First comes the special theory, then the general theory, and last a look at the universe as a whole.
Everyone believes they know what space and time are, because we live in them every day. Einstein shows that the way we measure them matters more than we think.
Physics is a science that trusts only what can be measured and tested. So every idea in this book is tied to something we can do or observe.
Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity had worked beautifully for more than two hundred years. They explained falling apples, rolling carts and the orbits of the planets.
In 1905 Einstein was a young clerk in the patent office in Bern, Switzerland. In his spare time he wrote the paper that gave the world the special theory of relativity.
The general theory was much harder to build than the special one. Einstein worked on it for years, often with great difficulty, and it reached its final form in 1915.
That, in a few words, is why the theory is called relativity. Motion is never measured on its own, only in relation to something else, such as the ground or a passing train.
Einstein starts his story with geometry, the school subject about points, lines and shapes. It is the oldest and most trusted science of space, so it is the best place to begin.
The word geometry comes from two Greek words that mean measuring the earth. It began as the practical craft of measuring fields, building walls and laying out roads.
About 2,300 years ago a Greek teacher called Euclid arranged geometry into one long chain of reasoning. Each statement in his chain rests on the ones that came before it.
At the start of the chain stand a few simple statements, called axioms, that are accepted without proof. One example says that two points have exactly one straight line passing through them.
From these axioms a clever student can prove one new theorem after another. The famous theorem of Pythagoras, about the squares on the sides of a right triangle, is one of them.
A good proof gives a feeling of complete certainty, as if no one could ever argue with it. That is why people have admired geometry for so long.
Yet suppose someone asks whether these statements are really true. The question is harder than it sounds, because words like point and line seem only loosely tied to real things.
In pure geometry a statement counts as true when it follows by logic from the axioms. That says nothing at all about whether it fits real rods, strings and fields.
To make geometry a science of the real world, Einstein ties its words to real things. A straight line becomes a tightly stretched string, and a distance becomes what a stiff rod measures.
Once the words mean real things, geometry turns into a branch of physics. Its statements can then be tested by measuring, like any other claim about nature.
For houses, roads and fields, the geometry of Euclid works wonderfully well. Einstein warns, however, that success in everyday life does not prove that it holds everywhere.
To say where something is, we always have to point to something solid and well known. If we say a cloud hangs above the Potsdamer Platz in Berlin, the square tells us where the cloud is.
We can say more by imagining a tall pole standing in the square and reaching up to the cloud. Its length tells us the height of the cloud, so now we know its place exactly.
In this way three numbers fix the cloud's position: how far along, how far across and how high. Such numbers are called coordinates, and any place in space can be described with three of them.
A ship's navigator does the same thing when he marks the position of his ship on a chart. The numbers are measured from the solid surface of the earth, which acts as his marker.
Physicists call the solid thing that we measure from a body of reference. The cloud, the ship and the stone all have positions only in relation to such a body.
Motion simply means that the position of an object changes as time goes by. So to describe it we need both a place, measured from a body of reference, and a time.
Einstein asks us to picture a man standing at the window of a moving railway carriage. Without throwing it, he lets a stone fall from the window onto the embankment beside the track.
The man in the carriage sees the stone fall in a straight line. A person standing on the embankment sees it fall along a curve instead.
So the path of the stone is not a fact about the stone alone. It has a meaning only when we say which body of reference it is measured from.
There is one more thing that these examples have taken for granted, and that is time. Einstein has used the word without explaining it, and he promises to come back to this gap later.
The law of inertia says that a body far away from all other bodies stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line. Its speed stays exactly the same until something comes along and pushes it.
This law does not hold for every body of reference, however. Those for which it holds are called Galilean, in honour of Galileo, and they play an important part in the theory.
A carriage rolling smoothly along a straight track is a good Galilean body of reference. But when the train brakes hard or turns a sharp bend, loose objects suddenly begin to slide or fall.
Einstein calls steady motion in a straight line, without rotation or jolts, uniform translation. Nothing speeds up, nothing slows down and nothing turns, so the ride feels perfectly smooth.
Now we can state the principle of relativity in its simple, restricted form. If the laws of nature hold in one Galilean body of reference, they hold in every other one moving steadily past it.

Long before Einstein was born, Galileo noticed something very similar about ships at sea. In a closed cabin below deck, no experiment with dripping water, flying insects or swimming fish can show whether the ship is moving steadily.
The Earth races around the Sun at about thirty kilometres every second, much faster than any train. Yet we feel nothing, because the motion is almost perfectly smooth and steady.
Now suppose a man walks forward along the corridor of a moving carriage. According to the old rule, his speed relative to the ground is the speed of the carriage plus his own walking speed.
If the train runs at a hundred kilometres an hour and the man walks at five, he moves at a hundred and five. If he walks backward through the carriage, the old rule gives him ninety-five instead.

This rule seems so obvious that it looks like plain common sense to almost everyone. But it quietly assumes that time and distance are the same for the train and for the ground, and nobody had questioned that.
In empty space light travels at about 300,000 kilometres every second. That is a speed so great that it is very hard for the human mind to picture.
Lightning shows how much faster light is than sound. We see the flash at once, but the thunder often reaches us many seconds later.
In just one second a beam of light could circle the whole Earth about seven times. Nothing else in everyday life comes anywhere near such a speed.
Light of every colour travels at exactly the same speed in empty space. The speed also does not depend on the lamp, the star or the flame that sent it out.
Einstein now asks us to picture a long, straight embankment with a railway track beside it. A ray of light runs along the embankment at its usual speed.
Next, a train races along the track in the same direction as the ray. A passenger sitting by the window wants to measure how fast the ray is travelling.
The old rule for adding speeds gives a clear answer. The passenger should find the speed of light minus the speed of the train, and so the ray should seem to go more slowly.

The principle of relativity, however, says that the laws of nature are the same on the train as on the embankment. If the law of light holds on the ground, it must also hold in the carriage, and the passenger should find the full speed.
Here we reach the heart of the puzzle, and it is a surprising one. The old rule for adding speeds says one thing, and the constant speed of light says another, so they cannot both be right.
Einstein decides not to give up either idea too quickly. Instead he asks what the old rule quietly assumes about time and distance, and whether those assumptions are really true.
When we say a train arrives at seven, we mean that the watch's small hand points to seven as it arrives. For an event right beside us, this idea of the same time causes no trouble at all.
For an event far away, however, the question becomes much harder. It is not at all clear what the same time can mean for something happening here and something happening in a distant place.
It does not help to look at a faraway clock through a telescope. The light needs time to arrive, and we can allow for the delay only if we already know how to measure time.
Suppose that two clocks of the same make stand far apart, one at A and one at B. They may tick at the same rate, but we still need a clear rule for setting them to show the same time.
Einstein offers a rule based on light: a flash goes from A to B and is reflected back to the first clock. The clocks count as set together if the trip there takes exactly as long as the trip back.

Now Einstein pictures two flashes of lightning that strike two places far apart on a long railway embankment. Let us call the places A and B, and let us ask whether the two strokes happened at the same time.
A man stands on the embankment exactly midway between A and B. If he sees the two flashes at the same moment, he says that they were simultaneous, because the light had equal distances to travel.
Meanwhile a train runs along the track, and a passenger sits at its middle. At the moment of the flashes he is level with the man on the bank, but he is moving toward the light from B.
Because the passenger rushes toward the light from B, he meets it first. He therefore says that stroke B came first, but the man on the bank says they were simultaneous.
Each of them is right in his own body of reference, and neither is making a mistake. There is no single now that holds for everybody, because every body of reference has its own time.
Finding the length of a rod seems the easiest thing in the world. If the rod lies still, we simply lay a ruler along it and read the numbers at its two ends.
A passenger on the train can do exactly this with a rod lying in the carriage. Since the rod moves along with him, he finds one clear answer for its length.

A man on the embankment has to work differently, because the rod is rushing past him. He marks the places where its two ends are at the same moment, and then he measures the distance between the marks.
Surprisingly, the two methods do not give the same answer. The man on the ground and the passenger disagree about which moments are simultaneous, and so they disagree about the length.

The Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz found a rule that turns one observer's measurements of place and time into another's. It is now called the Lorentz transformation, and Einstein shows that it follows from his two simple principles.
The rule has a result that sounds quite remarkable to most people. Seen from outside, a moving rod is shorter along its line of motion, and the faster it moves, the shorter it appears.
At about 260,000 kilometres a second, a moving rod would measure only half of its length at rest. As its speed came close to that of light, it would shrink toward nothing at all.
Moving clocks are affected in a similar way, and that is even stranger. As seen from outside, a clock that moves at that same great speed would tick at only half its usual rate.
To the passenger riding along, his own rod and clock look perfectly normal. The strange effects appear only when observers in different states of motion compare their results.
At the speed of an express train the effects are tens of thousands of times smaller than a single atom. That is why nobody ever noticed them in everyday life.
According to the theory, nothing can travel faster than light. The speed of light is therefore a kind of limit that no body of any kind can pass.
As a body comes closer to the speed of light, the strange effects grow stronger. Its length shrinks toward nothing, and a clock carried on it slows almost to a stop.

Speeds, it turns out, do not simply add up, and half plus half does not give the whole. A man walking at half light speed on a train moving at half light speed goes at only eight-tenths of light's speed.
The new rule always gives the same kind of answer. No matter which two speeds below the speed of light we combine, the result stays below the speed of light.
Now imagine that a very fast train sends a beam of light forward from a lamp. The passenger measures light at its usual speed, and so does the man standing at the station.
In 1851 the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau carried out a famous experiment. He sent beams of light through long tubes in which water was rushing along, some with the stream and some against it.
In still water light travels at about 225,000 kilometres a second, which is slower than in empty space. The old rule said that rushing water should add its own speed to this in full.
Fizeau found that the water carries the light along only partly. This agrees exactly with the new rule for adding speeds, so the experiment became strong support for the theory.

In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley, working in Cleveland in the United States, searched for the ether. This invisible stuff was supposed to carry light waves, but their careful experiment found no sign of the Earth moving through it.
Einstein shows that we do not need an ether at all. Light can travel across empty space without anything to carry it, and the speed of light is the same for every observer.
The special theory did not appear out of nothing. It grew from the theory of electricity and light by Maxwell and Lorentz, and it fitted the experiments already done.

In 1727 the English astronomer James Bradley noticed that the stars seem to shift a little during the year. The special theory explains this small movement in a simple way, because the Earth is moving while the light arrives.
The theory is also a useful guide for physicists. Every general law of nature must keep its form when it goes through the Lorentz transformation, and any law that does not must be wrong.
The theory brought a surprise about matter as well. A heated body, for example, takes in energy and becomes a little heavier, so mass and energy are one thing.

The energy held in a lump of matter equals its mass multiplied by the speed of light twice over. Because the speed of light is so large, even a very small mass stands for a very large amount of energy.

One gram of matter, which is about the weight of a small paper clip, holds as much energy as about twenty-five million kilowatt-hours. A family would need thousands of years to use as much electricity.
Radium gives off energy all the time as it slowly changes into other substances. In principle it loses a tiny amount of mass as it does so, although no scale could weigh the difference.
Before this, physicists had two great laws, one saying that mass is never lost and one saying that energy is never lost. Now the two become a single law, because mass and energy are the same thing.

In 1908 the German mathematician Hermann Minkowski, who had once been Einstein's teacher, made an important discovery. He showed that space and time can be joined together in one world of four dimensions.
To fix an event in this world we need four numbers: three to say where it happens and one to say when. Space and time are no longer two separate stages but a single whole.
The special theory covers only steady motion in a perfectly straight line. Einstein now asks whether a theory with such a narrow range can really be satisfying.
In the real world, motion is rarely so smooth. Cars speed up and brake, trains swing around bends, and the planets travel in curves.
In the old physics the Galilean bodies of reference are favoured. Only for them do the laws of nature take their simple, familiar form.
Einstein feels uneasy about this special treatment of one kind of motion. Nature gives no reason for preferring steady motion to every other kind, and a good theory should not make such a choice.

To make the point, Einstein borrows an example from the thinker Ernst Mach. Two fluid bodies float in empty space and turn around the line between them, and one of them is round while the other is flattened.
Newton's answer was that one of the bodies truly turns in absolute space. This is an invisible and unchanging stage that nobody has ever seen or touched.
Einstein finds this answer quite unsatisfying, and he says why. The cause of the flattening, he argues, should be something we can observe, not an unseen thing added to save the theory.
This leads him to the general principle of relativity. All bodies of reference, whatever their motion, should be equally good for stating the laws of nature.

To build such a theory Einstein must first understand gravity, the force that rules the old physics. Gravity acts on everything in the same way, and that curious fact seems to hold the key to the problem.
Newton's law of gravitation says that every body attracts every other body. The pull grows weaker as the distance grows, and it holds the Moon in its path around the Earth.
When we let a stone go, it falls to the ground. Physicists say that the Earth has a gravitational field, and the field pulls on the stone.
In air a feather drifts slowly down, while a coin drops quickly. But once the air is pumped out of a tall glass tube, the feather and the coin fall together.

A famous story says that Galileo dropped a heavy ball and a light ball from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. The story may only be a legend, but Galileo did show by careful tests that all bodies fall alike.
A heavy cart is hard to start and hard to stop, while a light one moves easily. The size of this resistance to being pushed is called the inertial mass of the body.
A heavy body is also pulled harder by the Earth than a light one. The size of this pull, which we feel as weight, depends on what is called the gravitational mass.
These two masses turn out to be exactly equal. A heavy body is pulled more strongly but resists more, so the two effects cancel, and all bodies fall alike.
The old physics simply accepted this equality as a plain fact and did not explain it. Einstein finds it strange that two ideas so different in meaning should always give equal numbers.
The Hungarian physicist Loránd Eötvös tested the equality with a very sensitive twisting balance. He found no difference at all between the two masses, to better than one part in a million.
Einstein thinks that nature is giving us a hint. A good theory, he believes, should explain the equality of the two masses, and not just accept it as a lucky chance.
The equal fall of all bodies suggests something even stranger. Gravity and a steady push may somehow be the same thing, and the next chapter shows why Einstein thought so.
Einstein now pictures a large chest, as big as a small room. It floats in empty space, far away from the stars and every other heavy body.
A being outside the chest fastens a rope to a hook on the lid. He pulls it with a steady force, so that the chest rises with ever-growing speed.
A man inside the chest feels the floor pressing against his feet. He stands there just as he would stand in a room on the surface of the Earth.
The man lets go of a stone, and it seems to fall to the floor. If he drops a feather or a heavy weight, they reach the floor together, so all bodies fall alike for him.
A watcher outside the chest tells a different story. For him the stone does not fall at all, because it is the floor that is rushing upward to meet it.

Neither man can prove the other wrong, and neither story is better than the other. From inside a closed chest, no experiment can tell gravity from acceleration, and this is called the principle of equivalence.
Now a weight hangs from a rope fixed to the ceiling of the chest. The man says that gravity pulls it down, while the outside watcher says that it resists being dragged upward.
This picture removes the old mystery about the two masses. The same property of a body shows itself both as its weight and as its resistance to being pushed.

Next, a ray of light crosses the chest from one wall to the other, travelling straight as the watcher outside sees it. But the chest rises while the light crosses, so for the man inside the ray curves downward.
If light curves in the accelerating chest, it should curve in a gravitational field as well. In a small room the bend is far too tiny to see, and only a huge mass such as the Sun could show it.
The general theory says that clocks run more slowly where gravity is stronger. On the Earth the difference is far too small for any ordinary person to notice.
To see how this changes geometry, Einstein pictures a large flat disc. It turns steadily around its centre in empty space, with an observer standing on it.
The person on the disc feels a force pushing him outward, away from the centre. By the principle of equivalence, this force is like a gravitational field.
The person wants to measure the edge of the disc and its width, just as a school student would. He uses small rods, laying them end to end as many times as he needs.
First he lays a rod along the width of the disc. The rod moves at right angles to its own length, so an observer outside sees no shortening, and the width comes out as usual.
Next he lays his rods one after another along the edge of the disc. They move along their own length, so they look shortened from outside, and more of them are needed.
The edge therefore measures more than the usual number multiplied by the width. This means that Euclid's geometry does not hold on the turning disc.
