Clocks behave in a strange way on the turning disc as well. A clock at the edge of the disc moves quickly, as seen from outside, so it runs more slowly than a clock at the centre.
The person on the disc agrees that a clock far from the centre runs slowly. In this gravitational field, then, time depends on place, and no single time suits the whole disc.
In such a field the old way of marking out place and time fails. Ordinary rods and clocks no longer give a simple map, and a new method is needed.
On a flat table top, Euclid's geometry works perfectly. Straight lines, right angles and triangles all behave in the usual way.
On a curved surface, such as a hill or a ball, things are different. We cannot lay straight rods side by side to make a perfect square grid.
On a globe a triangle can have three right angles. Start at the North Pole, go down to the equator, go a quarter of the way along it, and return.
A circle drawn on a ball also behaves oddly. If we measure along the surface, its rim is shorter than the usual number times its width.
Imagine flat creatures who live on a ball and cannot look up or down. By measuring circles and triangles in their world, they could still discover that it is curved.
The German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, who lived from 1777 to 1855, found a clever way to describe curved surfaces. His method needs no view from the outside at all.
Gauss laid a net of curves of any shape on the surface and gave each curve a number. Every point on the surface then has two numbers, like a street and a house number.
The distance between two nearby points can be worked out from their numbers. A rule that belongs to the surface itself tells us how, and no measuring rod is needed.
The net may be bent and stretched in any way, like a drawing on a rubber sheet. The whole geometry of the surface can still be found by using the numbers alone.
Gauss's pupil Bernhard Riemann went much further, in a famous lecture of 1854. He made a geometry for curved spaces with any number of dimensions, and Einstein would later put this idea to use.
In the special theory, space and time make up one four-dimensional world. Ordinary rods and clocks give the four numbers that fix any event in it.
In a gravitational field, rods and clocks no longer behave in the old way. The old method of giving numbers to events therefore breaks down.
Gauss's idea can be stretched to four dimensions, as Einstein now shows. It gives every event four numbers, in a net laid over space and time together.
These four numbers are only labels, much like house numbers in a street. The number that stands for time does not have to be read from a clock.
Any fair way of labelling events with four numbers is allowed. The net may be twisted and stretched as much as we please.
This leads to Einstein's general principle, which he states with care. It says that every Gaussian system of numbers is equally good for stating the general laws of nature.
A law of nature must therefore be written so that it keeps its form in every system of numbers. This demand is called general covariance, and it is a strong one.
The reason it works is that physics really records only meetings. Two particles arrive at the same point, or the hand of a clock reaches a mark on its face.
A meeting stays a meeting, whatever numbers we choose to give it. A crossroads is still a crossroads, whether it is drawn on one map or on another.
The price is that the numbers no longer mean lengths or times by themselves. A rule tells us how to turn them into distances, and with it the theory is ready for gravity.
In the general theory the geometry of the four-dimensional world is not the same everywhere. It changes from place to place, depending on the matter that is nearby.
The presence of matter curves the world around it. This curving is what we call gravity, and it is not a force reaching out across empty space.

A body left to itself follows the straightest possible path through the curved world. A marble rolling past a dent in a stretched sheet is a rough picture, although the real curving involves time as well as space.
A planet is not pulled by a rope from the Sun. It follows the straightest path through the world that the great mass of the Sun has curved.
In 1915 Einstein found the equations that link the curving of the world to the matter and energy in it. They are hard to solve, and they took him many years of work.
Where gravity is weak and speeds are slow, the new equations give almost exactly Newton's law of gravitation. That is why Newton's law worked so well for two hundred years.
The two laws are not quite identical, however, and Einstein says so plainly. The small differences between them can be tested by looking carefully at the sky.
Energy has mass, so light itself has a tiny weight. Gravity should therefore bend the path of a ray of light, just as the chest suggested.
The equations keep their form in every system of Gaussian coordinates. This means that the general principle of relativity is satisfied, as Einstein had hoped.
Near the Earth the world is almost flat, with very little curving. That is why Euclid's geometry works so well in schools and in building.
Einstein now turns to the universe as a whole. He asks how the stars are scattered through space, and what that tells us about its shape.
The old picture, built on Newton's ideas, took space to be endless and Euclidean. It had no limit in any direction, so that a traveller could go on for ever.
Suppose that all the stars form one great island in endless empty space. We can then ask what would happen to such an island over a very long time.
According to the old ideas, light and stars would slowly escape from the island into the void. The island would dwindle, and Einstein finds this hard to accept.
Suppose instead that stars are spread evenly through all of endless space. Then the universe would never thin out, and there would be no edge where the stars stop.
In that case, though, Newton's law gives only a muddle. The pull on any body from an endless supply of matter has no clear value.
The astronomer Hugo von Seeliger saw the trouble and suggested a cure. He proposed changing Newton's law so that gravity fades faster at great distances.
Einstein points out that this change was made up only to avoid the trouble. No fact observed in the sky supports it, so it is an unwelcome patch.
Both pictures lean on the idea that space is endless and Euclidean. But Euclid's geometry is now only one possibility among many.
Perhaps the universe can be limited in size without having any edge at all. This strange thought opens a new road, and the next chapter explores it.
The surface of a ball has a limited area, yet it has no edge. This is what is meant by finite but unbounded.
Flat creatures living on a ball could walk for ever without meeting a wall. Their world has a limited size, but they would never find a place where it stops.
They could draw circles in their world and measure them with rods. For big circles they would find that the rim is shorter than Euclid's geometry says it should be.
They could also measure triangles in their curved world, as a surveyor does. The three angles of a big triangle would add up to more than two right angles, which would reveal the curving.
On a very large ball, a small region looks almost perfectly flat. In the same way, people once believed that the Earth itself was flat, because they only saw a small part of it.
Our own space might be curved in a similar way, closed in on itself. We cannot picture this, but we can reason about it with rods and triangles, just as the flat creatures do.
In such a closed space a traveller who went straight on for ever would come back to the place where he started. It would be like sailing round the Earth, though in three dimensions.
In principle, even a ray of light would come back after a very long journey. The trip would take longer than any human being could ever imagine.
The size of a closed universe would depend on how much matter it holds. In 1916 the amount of matter in space was not known well enough to decide the question.
Whether our space is closed is a question for observation, and thought alone cannot settle it. Einstein offers it only as a possibility, which the future must test.
Johannes Kepler found that every planet travels in an oval path called an ellipse. The Sun stands not in the middle of the oval but at a special point inside it.
Newton's law explains very neatly what Kepler had found by patient work. For a single planet alone, it gives an ellipse that stays fixed and never turns.
Mercury is the planet nearest to the Sun, and it goes round very quickly. The point of its path that lies closest to the Sun is called the perihelion, and it is the key to this puzzle.
The pulls of the other planets, such as Venus and Jupiter, make Mercury's ellipse turn slowly round the Sun. Newton's law can work out how big this turning should be.
In 1859 the French astronomer Urbain Le Verrier checked the figures very carefully. He found that the real turning of Mercury's orbit is a little larger than Newton's law allows.
The leftover turning is only about 43 seconds of arc in a century. It is so small that a full extra turn would need about three million years.
Astronomers tried to explain it by imagining a planet called Vulcan, closer to the Sun than Mercury. They searched for it for years during eclipses, but they never found it.
In 1915 Einstein tried his new equations on a planet moving near the Sun. They gave just the extra turning that Mercury shows, with no adjustment at all.
The extra turning is smaller for planets farther from the Sun. This makes Mercury the best test of all, because it lies closest to the great mass.
The theory explained an old puzzle without any change or adjustment to make it fit. That made the success especially convincing, and it did not need any extra planet.
Einstein's theory makes a clear prediction that anyone can test. A ray of starlight that passes very close to the Sun should be bent by a little under two seconds of arc.
Stars near the Sun can be seen only during a total eclipse. Then the Moon hides the Sun, and the sky grows dark enough for the stars to appear.

The astronomers Frank Dyson and Arthur Eddington planned two expeditions to watch the eclipse of 29 May 1919. One went to the island of Principe, off West Africa, and the other went to Sobral in Brazil.
On Principe it rained that morning, and the observers feared the worst. The clouds thinned just before the eclipse, and Eddington's team managed to take their photographs.
The plates showed bright stars in the group called the Hyades. The astronomers compared them with plates of the same stars taken at night, when the Sun was far away.
In November 1919 the results were announced at a famous meeting in London. The stars seemed pushed outward by about the amount Einstein had predicted, although the measurements were not very exact.
Light that leaves a strong gravitational field is shifted slightly toward the red end of the spectrum. This was hard to measure in 1916, but later experiments confirmed it.
The theory removes Newton's idea of a still, absolute space as a fixed stage. It also removes the idea of a time that flows in the same way for everybody.

Despite its name, relativity says that light and nature's laws are the same for everybody. The special theory deals with steady motion, and the general theory adds gravity and every other kind of motion.

Einstein ends by hoping that his small book has given the reader some hours of pleasure and a taste for careful thought. Like every theory, his own stays open to new tests, and that is what makes it science.
C1C2: In 1916, in a Berlin crowded with the worries of a long war, Albert Einstein wrote a small book for readers who had no training in mathematics. His theory of relativity was already much discussed among scientists, yet almost nobody else could say what it claimed. He set out to change that with patient words, plain pictures and a handful of homely examples.

Einstein is honest from the first page about what he is asking of his readers. The language of his book is plain, he says, but plain words do not make unfamiliar ideas easy, and the reader will need patience and a good deal of will. In return he promises that no important step will be hurried past without an explanation.

Einstein builds his book like a staircase of three flights, each resting on the one below. The first deals with the special theory, which concerns steady motion; the second with the general theory, which brings in gravity; the third with the universe taken as a single whole. By the top, the reader has been carried from a railway embankment to the shape of space itself.

Space and time seem so familiar that we rarely ask what they are, yet we live inside them every moment of our lives. Einstein asks a simple but daring question: how do we actually measure them, with which rods and which clocks? The answer, he will show, quietly overturns what almost everyone has always taken for granted.

Physics differs from pure thought because in the end it must answer to the world as it really is. A statement about space or time means something, Einstein insists, only when we can say how it could be checked by a rod, a clock or a beam of light. This rule will guide him through the whole book, and it will lead him to some surprising places.

For more than two hundred years the physics of Isaac Newton had explained falling apples, rolling carts and the slow orbits of the planets with astonishing success. It seemed almost foolish to doubt a theory with such a record, and few people did. Yet a handful of small puzzles, especially about light, would not fit, and Einstein took them seriously enough to follow where they led.

In 1905, long before the world had heard his name, Einstein was a young clerk examining patent applications in the Swiss city of Bern. Out of working hours he thought about light, motion and time, and he published the paper that set out the special theory of relativity. It was one of several papers he wrote that year, and together they changed physics.

The general theory proved far harder to build than the special one, and it asked far more of its creator. Einstein struggled with it for years, filling notebooks, changing his mind and learning new kinds of mathematics along the way. It reached its final form in 1915, and the book you are reading was written soon afterwards.

The name relativity points to a simple fact that almost everyone already half knows. We can say how fast a thing moves only by comparing it with something else, such as the ground, a ship or a distant star. Einstein's task is to find out what follows when we take that simple fact completely seriously.

Einstein opens his argument not with stars or trains but with something every schoolchild has met, the geometry of points, lines and triangles. It is the oldest and most trusted science of space, taught in much the same way for well over two thousand years. If even that firm ground needs a second look, he suggests, then we should be ready for surprises.

The very word geometry comes from Greek words meaning the measuring of the earth, and that is how the subject began. Long before anyone wrote a proof, people needed to mark out fields, lay straight walls and share land fairly. The practical craft grew slowly into one of the most admired sciences in all of human history.

About 2,300 years ago a Greek teacher named Euclid gathered what was known of geometry and arranged it with remarkable care. His method was to build one long chain of reasoning in which each statement rests firmly on those that came before. The pattern proved so successful that it became a model for clear thinking in many other fields.

At the head of Euclid's chain stand a few simple statements, called axioms, which are accepted without proof because they seem too obvious to need any. One of them says that through any two points there passes exactly one straight line. Everything else in the subject is meant to be derived, step by careful step, from such humble beginnings.

From the axioms a patient student can derive theorem after theorem, each one resting securely on those before it. The best known, attributed to Pythagoras, states that the square on the longest side of a right triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two. It is surprising, it is useful, and once it has been proved it seems impossible to doubt.

A well-made proof gives the mind a feeling of complete certainty, as though no one on earth could ever argue with it. It is easy to see why so many thinkers have treated geometry as the finest example of sure knowledge. Einstein recalls that feeling himself, and then he asks the harder question of where such certainty actually comes from.

Yet suppose that someone stops the student and asks whether the statements of geometry are really true. The question is far harder than it sounds, because words such as point and line seem only loosely tied to anything we could actually find in the world. A mathematician may answer that the word true does not belong to geometry at all.

Within pure geometry a statement counts as true only in a narrow sense, namely that it follows by strict logic from the axioms. That is a claim about reasoning, not about the world, and it says nothing about whether the statement fits real rods, strings and fields. For a physicist, who wants to know about nature, the more interesting question is still unanswered.

To turn geometry into a science of the real world, Einstein ties each of its words to something we can handle. A straight line becomes the path of a tightly stretched string, a point becomes a tiny mark, and a distance becomes whatever a stiff measuring rod reports. With these links in place, the old statements suddenly say something definite about the world.

Once its words are tied to rods, strings and marks, geometry stops being pure thought and becomes a branch of physics. Its propositions can then be tested by measurement, exactly as one tests a claim about heat or electricity. If a careful measurement ever disagreed with Euclid, the world, not the textbook, would have the last word.

For houses, roads and fields the geometry of Euclid works so well that engineers and surveyors have relied on it for centuries. Einstein cautions, however, that success in everyday life is not proof that the rules hold everywhere, from the tiniest scale to the largest. That quiet warning looks modest now, but it will matter greatly later in his story.

To say where anything is, we must always point to something solid and well known. If we say that a cloud hangs above the Potsdamer Platz in Berlin, the great square gives the cloud a place by comparison, because it can be visited, measured and found again. The example is homely, but it already contains the idea on which the whole theory rests.

We can be more exact by imagining a tall pole that stands in the square and reaches up to the cloud. The length of the pole gives the height of the cloud, and the square itself fixes the spot on the ground beneath it. Together they pin down the cloud's position, which was only a vague gesture a moment ago.

In this way three numbers are enough to fix the position of the cloud: how far along, how far across and how high. Any place in space can be described by three such numbers, which are called its coordinates. That, in everyday terms, is what we mean when we say that space has three dimensions.

A navigator at sea uses the same idea when he marks the position of his ship on a chart. His numbers are measured from the solid surface of the earth, which serves as his marker just as the square did for the cloud. Whether we are sailors, builders or physicists, we cannot name a place without naming something to measure from.

Physicists give the solid thing that we measure from a rather grand name, the body of reference. The cloud, the ship and the stone each have a position only in relation to some such body, and if we change the body, the position changes with it. This simple remark is easy to accept now, and it will bear a great deal of weight before the book is done.

Motion, in the plainest terms, means that the position of an object changes as time goes by. To describe it we therefore need two kinds of information at once: a place, measured from a body of reference, and a moment in time. A moving thing is a series of places, each one tied to its own moment.

Einstein now asks us to picture a man standing at the window of a railway carriage that is rolling steadily along the track. Without throwing it, the man simply lets a stone drop from his hand and watches it fall toward the embankment. It is a trivial experiment, and yet it will teach us something important about how to speak of motion.

To the man in the carriage the stone falls in a perfectly straight line, straight down toward the ground. To a person standing on the embankment the very same stone falls along a curve, because it keeps moving forward with the train as it drops. Both observers are watching the same stone, and both are describing what they see correctly.

Einstein draws a conclusion that sounds simple but is deep: there is no such thing as the path of a body in itself. A path exists only in relation to a chosen body of reference, and each body of reference gives its own path for the same stone. To speak of the true path, without naming the body, is to say something that has no meaning at all.

There is one more ingredient in these examples that we have used without examining, and that ingredient is time. A moving stone has a position at each moment, yet what exactly is a moment, and how do we agree upon it for events in different places? Einstein admits that the word has been used carelessly so far, and he promises to repair the gap before the argument goes further.

The law of inertia, which goes back to Galileo and Newton, says that a body far removed from all other bodies stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed. A smooth ball on endless ice, with nothing to push or slow it, would roll on for ever without changing its course. Almost everything else in Newton's mechanics is built upon this quiet and modest first law.

This law does not hold for every body of reference, however, and that is a fact of great importance. A ball placed on the floor of a spinning fairground ride, for example, does not stay still or roll straight, but is flung outward. The bodies of reference for which the law of inertia does hold are called Galilean, and the whole of Newton's mechanics is written for them.

A railway carriage gliding smoothly along a straight track is, for practical purposes, a Galilean body of reference. Let the driver brake suddenly or send the train around a sharp bend, however, and loose objects begin to slide and tumble without any visible push. The law of inertia has stopped working, and the carriage has ceased to be a Galilean system.

Einstein calls steady motion in a straight line, without any rotation or jolting, uniform translation. Nothing in it speeds up, nothing slows down and nothing turns, so the ride feels as smooth as sitting in a quiet room. It is the simplest kind of motion, and the first theory deals with nothing more complicated.

Now we are ready to state the restricted principle of relativity in its familiar form. If the laws of nature hold in one Galilean body of reference, they hold equally well in every other Galilean body that moves steadily past it, whatever its speed. A physicist inside a smoothly moving train therefore has no way of discovering, by any experiment on mechanics, that the train is moving at all.

Long before Einstein was born, Galileo had noticed something very similar about ships at sea. In a closed cabin below deck, he wrote, no experiment with dripping water, flying insects or swimming fish can show whether the ship is sailing steadily or lying still in harbour. Everything inside behaves exactly as it would at rest, and only a glance at the shore could tell the difference.

The Earth itself races around the Sun at about thirty kilometres every second, far faster than any express train. Yet nobody feels the slightest push, because the motion is so nearly steady that, over short distances and times, the Earth behaves like a Galilean body of reference. This is the everyday meaning of the principle: a smooth ride, however fast, is invisible from the inside.

Now suppose that a man walks forward along the corridor of a carriage while the train runs steadily down the track. According to the old rule of mechanics, his speed relative to the ground is simply the speed of the carriage added to his own walking speed. It is the kind of arithmetic that every schoolchild carries out without a second thought.

If the train runs at a hundred kilometres an hour and the man strolls forward at five, then relative to the ground he is moving at a hundred and five. Should he turn and walk toward the back of the train, the same rule gives him ninety-five instead. Adding and subtracting speeds in this way seems as natural to us as counting coins in a purse.

This rule seems so obvious that it looks like pure common sense, and for centuries nobody thought to doubt it. Yet it rests on two quiet assumptions: that time passes at the same rate on the train and on the ground, and that lengths measured from either are the same. Einstein will challenge both, and the old rule will turn out to be only an approximation.

In empty space light travels at about 300,000 kilometres every second, a figure so vast that the human mind can scarcely picture it. It is the fastest thing known to physics, and it will turn out to be the hinge on which the whole theory swings. Everything that follows in this small book depends on taking that single number very seriously indeed.

Everyday life gives us a small hint of how swift light is, for we see a flash of lightning at once and hear its thunder only afterwards. Sound crawls through the air at about a third of a kilometre a second, so the rumble of a distant storm lags far behind its flash. Light, by comparison, seems to arrive in no time at all, as if the distance did not matter.

In a single second a beam of light could race around the whole Earth about seven times over. A message sent at such a speed would cross an ocean before we could draw a breath, and even the Sun's rays take only about eight minutes to reach us. Nothing in our ordinary experience comes anywhere near this extraordinary and almost unimaginable pace.

Light of every colour travels at precisely the same speed in empty space, from the deepest red to the faintest violet. The speed also seems to be independent of the lamp, the star or the flame that gave the light its start, and that is a very strange habit for a moving thing. Physicists had measured it again and again with great care, and the answer never changed in any way.

To bring this fact into the open, Einstein asks us to picture a long, straight embankment with a railway track running beside it. A ray of light speeds along the embankment, travelling at its usual immense speed, while the ground lies quietly beneath it. So far nothing could be simpler, or more familiar, to a reader who has watched trains go by.

Next, let a train race along the track in the same direction as the ray, with a passenger seated by the carriage window. The passenger takes out a stopwatch and a measuring line, and sets about discovering how fast the ray of light is travelling past the train. It is exactly the kind of experiment that a careful physicist might carry out.

The old rule for adding speeds gives a confident and perfectly clear answer to this question. The passenger, it says, should find the speed of light diminished by the speed of the train, so that the ray seems to creep along a little more slowly. Even a fast train would change the answer only slightly, but a slight change is still a change.

The principle of relativity, on the other hand, insists that the laws of nature are the same on the train as on the embankment. If the law that light always travels at one speed holds on the ground, it must hold in the carriage too, and the passenger must find the very same speed as the man standing on the bank. Both observers, in short, must write down the identical figure in their notebooks, whatever the train is doing.

Here, then, is the heart of the puzzle, laid bare in a few plain sentences. The old rule for adding speeds says one thing, the constant speed of light says another, and the two cannot both be right at once. Something that every physicist had believed for centuries will therefore have to be given up.

Einstein decides not to throw away either idea in a hurry, however, since each rests on a mountain of careful evidence. Instead he asks what the old rule quietly assumes about time and about distance, assumptions so natural that nobody had ever thought to write them down. By looking hard at those hidden assumptions, he begins to find a way out of the difficulty.

When we say that a train arrives at seven o'clock, we mean that the small hand of a watch pointing to seven and the arrival of the train happen together. For an event right beside us this idea of the same time causes no difficulty at all. We have used that idea every day of our lives, in kitchens and stations and schools, without a moment's doubt.

For an event far away, however, the question becomes a great deal harder, and ordinary habit gives us no help. What can it possibly mean to say that a rocket burst over distant hills at the same time as a clock struck in the valley? The words seem plain, yet their meaning begins to melt as we look at them.

It does not help to look at a distant clock through a telescope, because the light that carries its image needs time to reach us. The delay could be worked out only if we already knew how to measure time at both places, and that is exactly the knowledge we lack. We seem to be in danger of going round and round in a circle, using time to define the very thing we want to measure.

Suppose that two clocks of identical make stand far apart, one at a place A and one at a place B, each ticking at a perfectly steady rate. Even so, we still require an unambiguous rule for setting them so that they show the same time. Such a rule must be laid down by us, because nature does not hand one over ready made.

Einstein offers a rule that rests upon the behaviour of light and upon nothing else whatever. A flash leaves A, is reflected at B and returns to A, and the two clocks count as set together if the journey there takes exactly as long as the journey back. This is not a discovery but a definition, chosen because it is the simplest one possible.

Now Einstein pictures two flashes of lightning that strike two points far apart on a long railway embankment, and he calls the points A and B. He then asks a question that seems innocent: did the two strokes happen at the same time? The answer, as we shall see, turns out to depend entirely on the person who happens to be answering.

A man stands on the embankment at exactly the midpoint between A and B, and he watches for the two flashes. If they reach his eyes at the very same instant, he declares them simultaneous, since the light from each had an equal distance to travel at the same speed. By the definition we have just agreed upon, he is entirely correct in saying so, and nobody can fairly argue with him.

Meanwhile a train runs along the track in the direction from A to B, and a passenger sits in its middle. At the instant of the flashes he is level with the man on the embankment, but he is moving toward the light from B and away from the light from A. His motion therefore changes the order in which the two flashes reach his eyes, although the flashes themselves are unchanged.

Because the passenger is rushing toward the light from B, he meets that light a little before the light from A catches up with him. He therefore concludes, using the same definition and the same careful reasoning, that stroke B came before stroke A. The man on the bank, by contrast, insists that the two strokes were simultaneous.

Each of the two observers is right within his own body of reference, and neither has made the smallest mistake. There is therefore no single now that holds for everybody in the universe, because every body of reference has its own time. Without saying which body is meant, a statement about the time of an event has no meaning.

Finding the length of a rod seems to be the simplest task in the world, and nobody expects any trouble from it. If the rod lies still on a table, we lay a ruler alongside it and read off the numbers at its two ends. The whole business takes a moment and seems to leave no room for doubt.

A passenger on the train can do exactly the same with a rod lying on the floor of his carriage. Because the rod is carried along with him, it is at rest relative to the passenger, and he finds one clear and definite answer for its length. For him the measurement is as ordinary as it would be in a laboratory.

A man on the embankment has to proceed differently, because the rod is rushing past him at speed. He must mark on the ground the places where its two ends are located at the same moment, and then measure the distance between the two marks. What he means by the same moment, however, is precisely the definition that Einstein has just given.

Surprisingly, the two methods do not agree, and neither observer has made an error of any kind. The man on the ground and the passenger disagree about which moments are simultaneous, and so they inevitably disagree about the length of the rod. The difference lies not in their rulers or in their care but in their different ideas of time, which can no longer be called wrong.

The Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz had found a rule that turns one observer's measurements of place and time into another's, while keeping the speed of light the same for both. It is now called the Lorentz transformation, and Einstein shows that it follows naturally from his two simple principles. Lorentz had reached it by a longer road, still hoping to save the ether.

This rule has a remarkable and, at first sight, almost incredible result for anyone who measures moving things. Seen from outside, a moving rod is shorter along its line of motion than it is at rest, and the faster it moves, the shorter it appears. Its width across the line of motion, however, is not changed at all, and only the length along the motion shrinks.

At a speed of about 260,000 kilometres a second, which is a little under nine-tenths of the speed of light, a moving rod would measure only half of its length at rest. As its speed came closer and closer to that of light, it would shrink toward nothing at all. Light itself thus marks a boundary that no moving rod, and no moving body of any kind, can ever cross.

Moving clocks are affected in a similar way, which is perhaps even stranger than the shrinking of rods. As seen from outside, a clock that moves at that same great speed would tick at only half its usual rate, so that an hour on the ground would be only half an hour on the clock. Time, it seems, is not quite the same stuff everywhere, and it flows differently for those who move differently.

To the passenger riding along, his own rod and his own clock look perfectly normal, and he notices nothing odd in the carriage. The strange effects appear only when observers in different states of motion compare their results with one another. Each, moreover, finds the other's rods shortened and the other's clocks slow, so that neither observer can claim to be the one who is really at rest.

At the speed of an express train, the changes in length and time are tens of thousands of times smaller than the width of a single atom. That is why nobody noticed them for centuries, and why Newton's rules worked so well in everyday life. Only at speeds close to that of light do they grow large enough to be seen, measured and no longer ignored.

According to the theory, nothing at all can travel faster than light, whether it is a train, a rocket, a message or a particle of dust. The speed of light is therefore a kind of absolute limit, a ceiling that no body of any kind can ever pass. Physicists were slow to accept such a thought, but every careful experiment since has agreed with it.

As a body comes closer and closer to the speed of light, the strange effects described so far grow stronger and stronger. Its length along its line of motion shrinks toward nothing, and a clock carried on it slows almost to a stop. It would take more and more energy to speed it up by even a little, and the speed of light would still lie just out of its reach.

Speeds, it turns out, do not simply add up in the old way that every schoolchild has been taught to trust. If a train travels at half the speed of light and a man walks forward along it at half that speed, he moves not at the full speed of light but at only about eight-tenths of it. The simple sum of half and half, which works so well for walkers and for trains, does not hold when the speeds are large.

The new rule for combining speeds always delivers the same kind of answer, however large the speeds become. No matter which two speeds below the speed of light we choose to combine, the result stays below the speed of light, and only a beam of light itself can ever reach that top speed. The world, it seems, has a limit built into its very design, and no amount of effort can push past that limit.

Now imagine that a very fast train sends a beam of light forward from a lamp in its front carriage, racing toward a distant station. The passenger measures the beam and finds light moving at its usual speed, and so does the man waiting on the platform at the station. By the new rule these two measurements agree perfectly, which is something that the old rule for adding speeds could never allow.

In 1851 the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau carried out a famous experiment on how light behaves in a moving substance. He sent two beams of light through long tubes in which water was rushing along, one beam travelling with the stream and the other against it, and then compared them with delicate care. It was one of the finest experiments of its age, and its answer was not at all what most people had expected.

In still water light travels more slowly than in empty space, at about 225,000 kilometres a second. According to the old rule, water that is rushing along should add its own speed to this in full, so that the light would be carried onward like a swimmer on a fast current. Fizeau's careful measurements, however, showed something quite different from this simple and natural expectation.

Fizeau found that the flowing water drags the light along only partly, by less than half of its own speed. This is exactly what the new rule for adding speeds predicts, and the old rule cannot explain it, so the experiment, made long before the theory existed, became strong support for it. In science, agreement of that kind is worth more than any amount of clever argument.

In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley, working in Cleveland in the United States, searched for the ether, the invisible stuff that was supposed to carry light waves through space. They split a beam of light into two beams sent at right angles to each other and compared them. Their careful experiment found no sign that the Earth moves through any ether at all.

Einstein shows that we do not need an ether in order to understand light. A ray can travel across empty space without anything to carry it, and its speed is the same for every observer, however fast that observer may be moving. The ether, which had seemed so necessary to every physicist of the time, simply fades quietly out of the picture.

The special theory did not appear out of nothing, for it grew out of the theory of electricity and light developed by Maxwell and Lorentz. Einstein points out that it agrees with the experiments that had already been done, and that it removes the need for strange extra assumptions. It was less a revolution against the old physics than a clearing of its muddles.

In 1727 the English astronomer James Bradley noticed that the stars seem to shift a little in the sky in the course of a year, each tracing a tiny circle or oval. The special theory explains this small movement quite simply, because the Earth is moving while the light arrives. The movement is about twenty seconds of arc, a very small angle that only a telescope could detect.

The theory is also a useful guide for physicists who are still searching for the laws of nature. Every general law of nature must keep its form when it is put through the Lorentz transformation, so any proposed law that fails this test can be set aside as wrong. In this way the theory works like a sieve, catching the faulty laws before they do harm.

The theory brought a surprise about matter itself, and the surprise has been important ever since. A body that takes in energy, by being heated for example, becomes a little heavier, so mass and energy are really two forms of one and the same thing. The old division between stuff and force, which had seemed so firm and so obvious, quietly vanishes.

The energy held in any lump of matter equals its mass multiplied by the speed of light twice over, a rule that is now known to almost everybody. Because the speed of light is so enormous, even a very small mass stands for a staggeringly large amount of energy, locked up and almost always hidden. Only in rare and extreme processes can any real share of it be set free.

One gram of matter, about the weight of a small paper clip, holds as much energy as about twenty-five million kilowatt-hours of electricity. A family would need many thousands of years to use that much in its home, and yet it all lies in a tiny speck that seems to hold nothing. Ordinary changes, such as burning a lump of coal, release only the tiniest fraction of that hidden store.

Radium gives off energy continuously as it slowly changes into other substances, and it was the great marvel of its day. In principle it loses a tiny amount of mass as it does so, although no scale in the world could weigh so small a difference. Einstein suggested that such substances might one day be used to test the rule.

Before this discovery, physicists had held two great laws as sacred, one saying that mass is never lost and the other saying that energy is never lost. Now the two merge into a single law, because mass and energy turn out to be the same thing seen in two different ways. The result is simpler, grander and wholly in the spirit of science, which always hopes to explain more with less.

In 1908 the German mathematician Hermann Minkowski, who had once been Einstein's teacher in Zurich, made an important discovery about the special theory. He showed that space and time can be joined together in a single world of four dimensions, a stage on which every event has its own place. The idea changed the way that physicists talked about the universe, and it soon proved useful for much more than the special theory alone.

To fix the position of an event in this world we need four numbers: three to say where it happens and one to say when. Space and time are no longer two separate stages but a single whole, and a clock is as much a part of the map as a ruler. This picture would prove essential, as we shall see, when Einstein turned at last to the puzzle of gravity.

The special theory covers only steady motion in a straight line, and Einstein now asks whether a theory with so narrow a range can truly satisfy us. The theory is exact and beautiful within its limits, yet nature does not confine herself to smooth, straight journeys. A complete picture of the world, he feels, must say a good deal more than this one theory does.

In the real world, as every traveller knows, motion is rarely so smooth and gentle. Cars speed up and brake, trains swing around bends, and the planets themselves travel in curves around the Sun, so that very few things move exactly as the special theory requires. The restricted theory, however fine, leaves most of the world's motion outside its reach.

In the old physics, the Galilean bodies of reference are favoured above all the rest. Only for them do the laws of nature take their simple and familiar form, whereas for a spinning ride or a braking train the laws become tangled with strange extra forces. Physicists had grown so used to this privilege that they hardly noticed it, and few of them thought to complain.

Einstein feels uneasy about this special treatment of one kind of motion, and he cannot find a good reason for it. Nature gives no hint of preferring steady motion to every other kind, and a sound theory, he thinks, should not make such a choice without a cause. The favour shown to Galilean bodies looks to him like a flaw in the design of the whole subject, and one that deserves to be mended.

To make the point vivid, Einstein borrows an example from the Austrian thinker Ernst Mach. Two fluid bodies float in empty space, far from everything else, and they turn about the line between them; one of them is perfectly round, while the other is flattened like an orange. Why should two such bodies differ in shape, when each simply turns relative to the other?

Newton's answer was that the flattened body is the one that really turns in absolute space, an invisible and unchanging stage that nobody has ever seen or touched. Space itself, in his view, tells us which body is spinning and which is at rest. The explanation is clever, yet it rests on something that no one can observe.

Einstein finds this answer unsatisfying, and he says why with great clarity and with some force. The cause of the flattening, he argues, ought to be something that can actually be observed, and not an unseen thing that is added only to make the theory work. A true explanation, in his view, should rest on facts that anyone could in principle go and check for himself.

This line of thought leads him straight to the general principle of relativity, which is the grand aim of the second part of the book. All bodies of reference, whatever their motion, should be equally good for stating the laws of nature, and none should be favoured by the laws themselves. The path to such a theory, as he will now show, runs through the mystery of gravity.

To build such a theory Einstein must first understand gravity, the force that rules the motion of falling stones, swinging pendulums and planets alike. Gravity acts on everything in exactly the same way, and that curious fact seems to hold the key to the whole problem. It is the one force that every body feels in exactly the same manner, whatever it is made of or however heavy it may be.

Newton's law of gravitation says that every body in the universe attracts every other body, and that the pull grows weaker as the distance between them grows. It holds the Moon in its path around the Earth and the Earth in its path around the Sun, and for more than two hundred years no observation had seriously troubled it. Einstein's task is to improve it without destroying what it got right, and that is a delicate business.

When we let go of a stone, it falls to the ground, and nobody is surprised by this plain and familiar event. Physicists say that the Earth has a gravitational field, a region of space in which it can pull on other bodies, and the stone simply obeys the pull. Gravity is the name we give to whatever it is that makes the stone fall, and Newton gave it a law.

In ordinary air a feather drifts slowly downward while a coin drops quickly, and a careless observer might conclude that heavy things fall faster. But once the air is pumped out of a tall glass tube, a feather and a coin fall together and arrive at the bottom at the very same moment. The air, and not gravity itself, was getting in the way of the lighter object all the time.

A famous story says that Galileo dropped a heavy ball and a light one from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, and that both reached the ground together. The tale may well be only a legend, but Galileo did show by careful tests with rolling balls that all bodies fall alike. Modern measurements, made with far finer instruments, confirm his conclusion beyond any reasonable doubt.

A heavy cart is hard to start and just as hard to stop, while a light cart rolls away at the slightest touch. The size of this resistance to being pushed, which belongs to the body itself, is called its inertial mass. It is the mass that appears in Newton's law of motion, which links a push to the speeding up it causes.

A heavy body is also pulled harder by the Earth than a light one, which is why it feels heavier in the hand. The size of this pull, which we feel as weight, depends on what physicists call the gravitational mass of the body. It is the mass that appears in Newton's law of gravitation, which tells us how strongly two bodies pull on each other.

These two masses turn out to be exactly equal, and that fact is the whole secret of why all bodies fall alike. A heavy body is pulled more strongly by gravity but also resists being moved more strongly, so that the two effects cancel perfectly and the acceleration does not depend on the mass at all. The cancellation is exact, and that is why a stone and a boulder fall to the ground in the same time.

The old physics simply accepted this equality as a plain fact and offered no explanation for it. Einstein finds this strange, since the two ideas involved, resisting a push and being pulled by gravity, seem to have nothing to do with each other. Why should two quantities so different in meaning always come out exactly equal, whatever body we happen to weigh?

The Hungarian physicist Loránd Eötvös tested the equality with a very sensitive twisting balance, using bodies made of different materials. He found no difference at all between the two kinds of mass, to better than one part in a million, and later experiments pushed the accuracy even further. Nature, it seems, does not allow even the smallest gap between the two kinds of mass, however closely we look.

Einstein believes that nature is giving us a hint, and that it would be foolish to ignore it. A good theory, he feels, should explain the equality of the two masses and not simply accept it as a lucky accident of the world. A law that cannot say why it holds, he thinks, is only half a law, and it leaves the best part of the story untold.

The equal fall of all bodies suggests something even stranger than a lucky accident. Gravity and a steady push may somehow be the same thing in disguise, and the next chapter shows with a famous thought experiment why Einstein came to think so. It is one of the most fruitful ideas in the whole of modern physics, and Einstein called it the happiest thought of his life.

Einstein now asks the reader to picture a large chest, as big as a small room, floating in empty space. It is so far from every star and every other heavy body that no gravity can be felt there at all. Everything inside it would float freely, like dust in a sunbeam, and no object could be said to have any weight at all.

A being outside the chest fastens a rope to a hook on the middle of its lid and begins to pull. He pulls with a constant force, so that the chest rises with ever-growing speed, always accelerating in the same direction. It is a simple arrangement, and everything that matters in this part of the argument will follow from it in due course.

A man inside the chest feels the floor pressing steadily against the soles of his feet, as though the chest were resting on the ground. He can stand there, walk about and lean against the walls, exactly as he would in any room on the surface of the Earth. Nothing in his experience gives him even the smallest hint that anything unusual is going on around him.

The man lets go of a stone, and it seems to him to fall to the floor, just as a stone would fall in a house on Earth. If he drops a feather and a heavy weight together, they reach the floor at the same moment, so that all bodies fall alike for him too. He naturally concludes that he is standing in a gravitational field, and he sees no reason to suppose otherwise.

A watcher outside the chest, who can see everything from his place in empty space, tells a quite different story. For him the stone does not fall at all, since once released it simply drifts onward, and it is the floor of the chest that rushes upward to meet it. Both accounts describe the very same event, but they describe it in different languages, and each language has its own logic.

Neither man can prove the other wrong, and Einstein draws a bold conclusion from this fact. From inside a closed chest, no experiment of any kind can tell the pull of gravity from the effect of a steady acceleration, and this is called the principle of equivalence. Gravity and acceleration, in this small region at least, are two descriptions of one and the same thing, and the choice between them is only a matter of taste.

Now a weight hangs from a rope fixed to the ceiling of the chest, and the rope is pulled tight. The man inside says that gravity drags the weight downward, while the watcher outside says that the weight, by its inertia, resists being dragged upward along with the chest. The two explanations agree in every detail of the outcome, and no measurement could ever favour one over the other.

This picture removes the old mystery about the two masses, which had troubled physicists for so long. The same property of a body shows itself both as its weight in a gravitational field and as its resistance to being pushed, so the two masses must be equal. What had looked like a deep puzzle turns out, quite unexpectedly, to be a simple and natural consequence of the picture.

Next a ray of light crosses the chest from one wall to the other, and the same two observers describe what happens. To the watcher outside, the ray travels in a straight line, but since the chest rises while the light crosses, the ray hits the far wall lower than it started. To the man inside, the ray therefore seems to curve downward, just like a stone thrown sideways across the room.

If light curves in the accelerating chest, then it should curve in a gravitational field as well, for the two situations cannot be told apart. Across a small room the bending is far too tiny to see, since the light crosses it in a few billionths of a second, and only a huge mass such as the Sun could show it. That, as we shall see, became one of the great tests of the theory, and it was carried out in the year 1919.

The general theory says that clocks run more slowly where gravity is stronger, so that a clock at the foot of a tower ticks a trifle slower than one at its top. On the Earth the difference is far too small for any ordinary person to notice, but in principle it is real. Einstein will soon show why it must be so, using nothing more than a spinning disc and a little patient thought.

To see how gravity changes our ideas about geometry, Einstein pictures a large flat disc that turns steadily around its centre in empty space. A person stands on the disc, carrying small rods and a clock, and he is determined to find out how the world looks from his turning platform. Another observer, who does not turn at all, watches the whole scene from his own place outside the disc.

The person on the disc feels a force pushing him outward, away from the centre, and the farther from the centre he stands, the stronger it is. By the principle of equivalence, he may regard this force as a gravitational field that acts on everything on the disc. He and his little world have a gravity of their own, and it is a gravity that comes entirely from their turning.

The person wants to measure the edge of the disc and its width, exactly as a school student would measure a circle drawn on paper. He uses small rods of equal length, laying them end to end as many times as he needs, and then he divides one total by the other. The experiment is the plainest one that geometry could ask for, and nobody would expect it to cause any trouble.

First he lays a rod along the width of the disc, from the rim through the centre. Since the rod moves at right angles to its own length, the observer outside sees no shortening of it, and the width comes out exactly as in the old school geometry. So far there is nothing at all to surprise him, and he may think that his old geometry is quite safe.

Next he lays his rods along the edge of the disc, one after another around the circle. These rods move along their own length, so the outside observer sees them shortened, and the person on the disc therefore needs more of them to go all the way around. The rim comes out noticeably longer than he expected, and no amount of careful counting will make it shorter.

The edge of the disc therefore measures more than the usual number, about three and a seventh, multiplied by the width, and the discrepancy is no mistake of measurement. This means that Euclid's geometry does not hold on the turning disc, and by equivalence it does not hold in a gravitational field either. The old geometry, the pride of two thousand years of careful thought, has met something that it cannot easily explain.

Clocks behave strangely on the turning disc too, and for a reason very like the one that shrinks the rods. A clock at the edge of the disc moves quickly, as seen from outside, and therefore runs more slowly than a clock at the centre, where there is almost no motion. The farther from the centre a clock is placed, the more slowly it ticks.

The person on the disc agrees with this verdict, since he can compare the clocks by exchanging signals. In this gravitational field, then, time depends on place, and no single time suits the whole disc, whatever the observer may wish. What is true of the time at the edge of the disc is simply not true of the time at its centre, and nobody can say otherwise.

In a gravitational field, therefore, the old way of marking out place and time with ordinary rods and clocks fails completely. Rods change their lengths with their position, clocks change their rates, and the whole neat grid of the older physics bends and wrinkles. A new method of describing positions is needed, and the mathematician Gauss, as we shall see, had already invented one.

On a flat table top, Euclid's geometry works perfectly, and nobody who has ever drawn a triangle with a ruler would doubt it. Straight lines, right angles and the sums of angles all behave in the usual and familiar way. It is the geometry of the classroom, and for centuries it seemed to be the geometry of the world.

On a curved surface, such as a hill or the skin of a ball, things are different, and the difference shows itself at once. We cannot lay straight rods side by side to make a perfect square grid, for the rods would either overlap or leave gaps. The curve of the surface forbids the neat pattern that a flat surface allows.

On a globe, a triangle can have three right angles, which is impossible in Euclid's flat geometry. Start at the North Pole, go straight down to the equator, travel a quarter of the way along it, and then come straight back up to the pole, and the three corners of your journey are all square. The angles of this triangle add up to more than two right angles, a clear sign that the surface is curved.

A circle drawn on a ball also behaves oddly, as any globe-maker could tell us. If we measure its width along the surface and compare it with its rim, we find that the rim is shorter than the usual number multiplied by the width. The larger the circle is, the greater the shortfall becomes, until the rim has shrunk well below what we expect.

Imagine flat creatures who live on the surface of a ball and cannot look up or down. They could still discover that their world is curved, simply by measuring the circles and triangles that they find in it, and comparing the results with Euclid's rules. Einstein will later suggest that we might do the same with our own space.

The German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, who lived from 1777 to 1855, found a clever way to describe a curved surface without ever leaving it. His method needs no view from the outside, and it needs no flat table on which the surface could be unrolled. It is a way of knowing a whole world from within, using nothing but the numbers that belong to it.

Gauss laid a net of curves of any shape on the surface and gave each curve its own number, in much the way that streets are numbered in a town. Every point on the surface then has two numbers, one from each of the two sets of curves that cross there. These two numbers are its Gaussian coordinates, and they serve as its address, telling us exactly where on the surface it lies.

The distance between two neighbouring points can be worked out from their numbers, as Gauss proved, by a rule that belongs to the surface itself. The numbers are not themselves lengths, and no measuring rod is needed to read them, but the rule turns them into true distances. In this way the geometry of the surface is hidden inside a table of numbers.

The net may be bent and stretched in any way, like a drawing on a rubber sheet that is pulled this way and that. The whole geometry of the surface can still be found by using the numbers alone, together with the rule that turns them into distances. No particular net is better than any other, and that fact is the key to what follows.

Gauss's pupil Bernhard Riemann went further in 1854, in a famous lecture that few people at first understood. He made a geometry for curved spaces with any number of dimensions, not only for surfaces, and Einstein would later put this idea to work. Without Riemann's mathematics, the general theory of relativity could hardly have been built, and Einstein was glad to learn it from his friend Grossmann.

In the special theory, space and time make up one four-dimensional world, as Minkowski showed, and ordinary rods and clocks give the four numbers that fix any event in it. Everything is simple because the bodies of reference are Galilean, and rods stay the same length wherever they are laid. The geometry of this world is as straightforward as the geometry of Euclid, and nobody needs any special tools to work in it.

In a gravitational field, however, rods and clocks no longer behave in the old way, as the turning disc has shown. Their lengths and rates depend on where they are, and the old method of giving numbers to events by reading rods and clocks therefore breaks down. Something more flexible and more general must now take its place, if the theory is to reach all kinds of motion.

Gauss's idea can be stretched from surfaces to the four-dimensional world, and Einstein stretches it. It gives every event four numbers, in a net laid over space and time together, just as two numbers fixed every point on the curved surface. The net is a mathematical convenience, drawn only in the mind, and it is certainly not a thing made of rods and clocks.

These four numbers are only labels, much like the house numbers in a street, and they need not mean anything more. The number that stands for time does not have to be read from a clock, and the numbers for place do not have to be lengths measured with a rod. They have to do nothing at all except tell different events apart, so that each event has a name of its own.

Any fair way of labelling events with four numbers is therefore allowed, however much the net is twisted, stretched or squeezed. Two physicists may choose quite different nets and still describe the very same world, as two mapmakers may draw the same coast with different grids. Nature does not care which grid we use, and the laws we write down should not care either.

This leads directly to Einstein's general principle of relativity, which he states in very careful words. It says that all Gaussian coordinate systems are essentially equivalent for stating the general laws of nature, so that no system is better than any other. This is a far wider freedom than the special theory ever gave, since it takes in every kind of motion, steady or not.

A law of nature must therefore be written in such a way that it keeps its form in every system of numbers, whichever net we lay over the world. This demand is called general covariance, and it is a strong one, since it rules out any law that depends on a favoured grid. It also guides the search for the laws themselves, because only laws of the right shape can be true in the general theory.

The reason that such a freedom is possible is that physics really records only meetings, which Einstein calls coincidences. Two particles arrive at the very same point at the very same moment, or the hand of a clock reaches a mark on its face, and these are the facts that observation can ever confirm. Everything else, in the end, is only bookkeeping, a way of keeping track of the meetings that nature has actually arranged.

A meeting stays a meeting, whatever numbers we choose to give it, and nothing about the event itself changes. A crossroads is still a crossroads, whether it is drawn on one map or on another, and two travellers who arrive there together still meet. Physical truth lies in such meetings, in what really happens, and not in the labels that we happen to attach to them.

The price of this freedom is that the numbers no longer mean lengths or times by themselves, so that a rule is needed to turn them into distances. With that rule in hand, however, the theory is ready for gravity, and the next chapter shows how gravity fits into it. The stage is now set, the actors are in their places, and the great idea can at last be stated in a few plain words.

In the general theory, the geometry of the four-dimensional world is not the same everywhere, as it was in the special theory. It changes from place to place, depending on the matter that happens to be nearby, and it must be found by measurement and calculation. The world has a shape of its own, and that shape responds, like a stretched sheet, to whatever heavy things are placed upon it.

The presence of matter curves the world around it, and this curving is what we call gravity. Gravity is no longer a mysterious force reaching out across empty space, as Newton had pictured it, but a property of the geometry of space and time themselves. It is a bold change of viewpoint, and an extraordinarily fruitful one, as the rest of this book will show.

A body left to itself follows the straightest possible path through the curved world, and it needs no force to tell it where to go. A marble rolling past a dent in a stretched rubber sheet gives a rough picture of this, although the real curving involves time as well as space, and no picture can be exact. The straightest path in a curved world is not what we would call a straight line, but it is as straight as the world allows.

A planet is therefore not pulled along by a rope from the Sun, but follows the straightest path through the world that the great mass of the Sun has curved. It circles the Sun for the same reason that a marble circles a funnel, because that is simply the way that the shape of the world leads it. The planet is doing nothing except going as straight as the curved world allows it to go, for that is all that any free body can do.

In 1915, after years of hard labour and false starts, Einstein found the equations that link the curving of the world to the matter and energy it contains. They are very difficult to solve, and few people could follow their derivation without years of training in mathematics. Yet the idea behind them can be stated in a sentence: matter tells the world how to curve.

Where gravity is weak and speeds are slow, the new equations give almost exactly Newton's law of gravitation, which is a most reassuring result. That is why Newton's law worked so well for two hundred years, and why it is still used today to send rockets to the Moon. Einstein's theory does not throw away the old one but contains it as a special case.

The two laws are not identical, however, and Einstein is careful to say so. The small differences between them can be tested by looking carefully at the sky, where gravity acts over great distances and in strong fields. A theory that makes new predictions can be proved wrong, and that is the best kind of theory.

Energy has mass, as the special theory showed, so light itself must have a tiny weight. Gravity should therefore bend the path of a ray of light, just as the thought of the chest suggested, although the bending is very small. A ray grazing the Sun, the strongest source of gravity near us, should be turned by only a tiny angle.

The equations keep their form in every system of Gaussian coordinates, whatever net we lay over the world. This means that the general principle of relativity is satisfied, just as Einstein had hoped when he first set out to find a theory that treated all motion alike. The mathematics and the principle fit each other like a hand in a glove.

Near the Earth the world is almost flat, with very little curving, since the Earth's gravity is weak in the sense that matters here. That is why Euclid's geometry works so well in schools, in building and in surveying, and why nobody noticed the curving for two thousand years. The curving, though real, is much too small to be seen with a ruler.

Einstein now turns from falling stones and spinning discs to the universe as a whole, and the change of scale is dizzying. He asks how the stars are scattered through space, and what the answer might tell us about the shape and size of the world. It is a question that astronomers of his day could only begin to answer, and a good deal remains open even now.

The old picture, built on Newton's ideas, took space to be endless and Euclidean, with no limit in any direction whatever. A traveller could set out toward the stars and go on for ever without reaching a wall, a boundary or an edge. Most people had accepted this picture so completely that they hardly thought of it as a choice.

Suppose, for the sake of argument, that all the stars form a single great island in endless empty space, surrounded on every side by emptiness. Einstein then asks what would happen to such an island over a very long time. The question seems innocent enough at first sight, but the answer turns out to be rather awkward for the old theory.

According to the old ideas, light and stars would slowly escape from the island and drift away into the void, never to return. The stellar system would therefore dwindle, losing its energy and its matter little by little, and in the end very little would remain. Einstein finds it hard to believe that the world is built in such a way.

Suppose instead that stars are spread evenly through all of endless space, so that the universe never thins out anywhere. Then there would be no island and no edge, and the stars would continue in every direction for ever. This seems a much more natural picture, until we try to apply Newton's law to it.

In that case Newton's law gives only a muddle, for the pull on any body from an endless supply of matter has no clear value at all. Mathematically the pulls from different directions add up in a way that cannot be settled, and no definite force results. A law that cannot give a definite answer to so simple a question has plainly run into a serious problem of its own.

The astronomer Hugo von Seeliger saw this difficulty and suggested a cure, which was to change Newton's law of gravitation slightly. He proposed that gravity should fade away faster than usual at very great distances, so that the pulls of the far stars could be kept under control. The change was small, and it seemed to solve the problem on paper, so that some astronomers were quite satisfied with it.

Einstein points out that this change was made up only to avoid the trouble, and that nothing seen in the sky supports it. A rule invented merely to rescue a theory has no strength of its own, and a good physicist should distrust it. The patch is an unwelcome one, and he prefers to look for a deeper cure.

Both pictures lean on the idea that space is endless and Euclidean, and that is the assumption that Einstein now wishes to question. After the lessons of the turning disc, Euclid's geometry is only one possibility among many, and it may not be the one that nature has chosen. If so, the old difficulties may simply vanish, like a shadow when a lamp is carried into the room.

Perhaps the universe can be limited in size without having any edge at all, which sounds like a contradiction but is not. This strange thought opens a new road for the imagination, and the next chapter explores it with the help of a ball and some flat creatures. It is one of the most beautiful ideas in the whole book, and it is also one of the hardest to picture.

The surface of a ball has a limited area, yet it has no edge anywhere, and that is what is meant by saying that it is finite but unbounded. Nobody who walks on it ever reaches a boundary or a wall, and still the whole surface could be covered with a finite amount of paint. The paradox disappears as soon as we see that the surface is curved, bending back on itself and closing without any seam.

Flat creatures living on the surface of a ball could walk for ever without meeting a wall, even though their whole world has a limited size. Each of them would be free to set out in any direction and to go on as long as it liked, and yet no creature would ever find a place where the world came to an end. Such a world would feel endless to those who lived in it, although a visitor from outside could see its whole size at a glance.

The creatures could draw circles in their world and measure them with their rods, using the same methods as a surveyor on a flat field. For small circles the usual rules would hold, but for big circles they would find that the rim is shorter than Euclid's geometry says it should be. Something about their world would then be telling them that it is not flat.

They could also measure triangles, and the results would be just as revealing as the circles. The three angles of a large triangle would add up to more than two right angles, and the larger the triangle, the greater the excess would be. In this way, without ever leaving their surface, the creatures could discover that their world is curved.

On a very large ball, a small region looks almost perfectly flat, and the creatures might never notice the curving unless they measured over great distances. In the same way, people for centuries believed that the Earth itself was flat, because they saw only a small corner of it at a time. The roundness was there all along, but it was too gentle to be seen by anyone who stayed near home and looked only at the ground.

Our own space might be curved in a similar way, closed in on itself like the surface of a ball but with one dimension more. We cannot picture this, since our minds are used to flat space, but we can reason about it with rods and triangles, just as the flat creatures reason about their world. Mathematics can go where the imagination cannot follow, and it is mathematics that lets Einstein speak of such a space.

In such a closed space a traveller who went straight on for ever would come back to the place where he had started, from the opposite direction. It would be like sailing round the Earth, though in three dimensions and on a far grander scale, and he would never meet an edge or a wall on his way. He would simply find himself at home again, tired but quite certain that he had never once turned round.

In principle, even a ray of light would come back after a very long journey, having travelled all the way round the universe. The trip would take longer than any human being could imagine, and the light would have to be very faithful to its course. Still, the possibility follows quite naturally from the geometry, and it would be wrong to rule it out in advance.

The size of a closed universe would depend on how much matter it holds, since the more matter there is, the more strongly the space is curved and the smaller the whole becomes. In 1916 the amount of matter in space was not known well enough to decide the question, and Einstein says so honestly. Here the theory must simply wait for the astronomers, whose telescopes alone can tell us how much matter fills the sky.

Whether our space is closed or open is a question for observation, and thought alone cannot settle it, however clever the thinker. Einstein offers the idea only as a possibility that the future must test, and he does not claim that the universe is known to be closed. That honesty about what is still unknown is a large part of the book's charm, and of its lasting value to the reader.

Johannes Kepler found, after years of patient calculation, that every planet travels in an oval path called an ellipse. The Sun stands not in the middle of the oval but at a special point inside it, and the planet moves faster when it is nearer the Sun. Kepler's discovery, which he published in the early years of the sixteen hundreds, was one of the great achievements of early astronomy.

Newton's law of gravitation explains what Kepler had found, and it explains it beautifully. For a single planet moving alone around the Sun, it gives an ellipse that stays fixed in space and never turns, so that the planet traces the same oval for ever. The picture was clean and simple, and astronomers were justly proud of it for more than two hundred years after Newton.

Mercury is the planet nearest to the Sun, and it goes round it very quickly, taking only about eighty-eight days. The point of its path that lies closest to the Sun is called the perihelion, and it is the key to this puzzle. Where that point lies in the sky, and how it moves from one century to the next, can be measured with very great care.

In reality, no planet moves alone, and the pulls of the other planets, such as Venus, Earth and Jupiter, make Mercury's ellipse turn slowly round the Sun. Newton's law can work out how big this turning should be, and the calculation was carried out with great skill. Most of the turning that astronomers observe is accounted for in this way, but not quite all of it.

In 1859 the French astronomer Urbain Le Verrier, who had already predicted the planet Neptune from its pull on Uranus, checked the figures with great care. He found that the real turning of Mercury's orbit is a little larger than Newton's law allows, and that no known planet could account for the difference. The puzzle of Mercury had begun, and it was to remain unsolved for more than half a century.

The leftover turning is only about 43 seconds of arc in a century, where a second of arc is the three-thousand-six-hundredth part of a degree. It is so small that a full extra turn would need about three million years, and yet astronomers could measure it, and it would not go away. A tiny discrepancy of this kind can be the sign of a deep mistake in the theory that fails to explain it.

Astronomers tried to explain the leftover by imagining a planet, which they called Vulcan, circling closer to the Sun than Mercury and tugging on it. They searched for it for years, especially during eclipses when the sky near the Sun grows dark, but they never found it. By the time of Einstein's book, most astronomers had given up the hunt, and the planet is now known never to have existed.
