In 1915 Einstein tried his new equations on a planet moving near the Sun, and he found that they give just the extra turning that Mercury shows. No adjustment was needed, no extra planet and no change to the constants of the theory, and the answer came out right on the first attempt. By his own later account, Einstein was beside himself with joyful excitement for several days.

The extra turning predicted by the theory is smaller for planets farther from the Sun, where the curving of the world is gentler. Mercury, which lies closest to the great mass of the Sun, is therefore the best test of all, and the effect is far too small to measure for the outer planets. It was Mercury's luck, and Einstein's too, to lie so near to the Sun that its small effect could be measured at all.

The theory explained an old puzzle without any change or adjustment to make it fit, and this made the success especially convincing. Seeliger's patch for the universe had been invented to save a theory, but here the theory was left alone, and the answer simply appeared out of the equations, without any help from the person who was doing the sums. Such a result is exactly the kind that physicists find hardest to resist, since it was neither expected nor arranged in advance.

Einstein's theory makes a clear and rather daring prediction about the way that light behaves in the sky. A ray of starlight passing very close to the Sun should be bent by a little under two seconds of arc, which is twice as much as a simple use of Newton's ideas would suggest. The prediction could be tested, and a wrong answer would have ended the theory, so Einstein was taking a real risk.

Stars close to the Sun can be seen only during a total eclipse, when the Moon covers the glaring disc of the Sun and the sky grows dark enough for the stars to appear. Then a photograph of the stars around the Sun can be compared with a photograph of the same stars taken at night. Any shift in their positions, however small, would show the bending of the light and prove the theory right.

The astronomers Frank Dyson and Arthur Eddington planned two expeditions to watch the great eclipse of 29 May 1919. One went to the island of Principe, off the coast of West Africa, and the other to Sobral in Brazil, so that bad weather at one place would not ruin the whole test. It was a bold and carefully planned undertaking, and it was made just after the end of a terrible and exhausting war.

On Principe it rained that morning, and the observers feared that the clouds would hide the eclipse altogether. The clouds thinned just before the Sun was covered, and Eddington's team managed to take their photographs in the short time that the darkness lasted. Years of planning and a great deal of money depended on those few precious minutes of darkness, and nothing could be repeated.

The plates showed the bright stars in the group called the Hyades, which lies in the constellation of Taurus and happened to stand near the Sun on the day of the eclipse. The astronomers compared them with plates of the same stars taken at night, when the Sun was far away in another part of the sky. Then they measured the tiny differences between the two sets of plates with great patience, over many weeks of work.

In November 1919 the results were announced at a famous meeting in London, and the news spread around the world. The stars seemed to be pushed outward from the Sun by about the amount that Einstein had predicted, although the measurements were not very exact and some scientists remained cautious. Later eclipses, observed with better instruments, gave better results, and they supported the theory more and more strongly.

Light that leaves a strong gravitational field, such as the light of the Sun, is shifted slightly toward the red end of the spectrum, because clocks run more slowly where gravity is stronger. This effect was very hard to measure in 1916, and Einstein is careful to say so, but later experiments, with far finer instruments, confirmed it beyond doubt. Another prediction of the general theory had passed its test, and the theory stood a little more firmly than before.

The theory removes Newton's idea of a still, absolute space that serves as a fixed stage for everything that happens. It also removes the idea of a time that flows in the same way for everybody in the universe, whatever their motion or their place. In their stead we have a world of events, whose shape depends on the matter it contains, and whose laws are the same for all.

Despite its name, relativity does not say that everything is relative, and Einstein is anxious that his readers should understand this. It says that the speed of light and the laws of nature are the same for everybody, and that it is only our ordinary ideas of space and time that must be revised. The special theory deals with steady motion, and the general theory adds gravity and every other kind of motion.

Einstein closed his book with the hope that it would give its readers a few hours of real pleasure and a taste for careful thought, even if they never touched the mathematics behind it. A theory such as his, however beautiful, remains open to new tests, and it must be given up if the world refuses to agree with it. That honest readiness to be checked is what makes the theory not a belief but a piece of science, and it is why the story has not stopped.
